messages.subject: Convergence in all parameters, apart from the log-probability
messages.subject_clean: Convergence in all parameters, apart from the log-probability
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have been working on a particular model, and am finding that there is convergence in all parameters (Rhat < 1.1), apart from the log-probability which remains (stubbornly) not so (Rhat ~ 10).

This, to me at least, is a new occurrence, and I am not sure what it means/how-to-remedy the situation. Does anyone have any ideas on this? Answers from both from a theoretic (why can this happen?) and practical standpoint (what should I do about it?) would be useful.

Best,

Ben

> > Thanks for sending the code. I haven't been able to replicate the problem you mentioned, so I'm not sure what happened when you were getting those errors. The model as you have it now seems to work ok, but not great. In particular the Rhats and effective sample sizes for lp__ and sigma_epsilon are a bit concerning.
> >
> > Instead of epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma_epsilon), I would suggest defining the epsilon vector in transformed parameters as the product sigma_epsilon * epsilon_raw, where epsilon_raw is declared in the parameters block, is the same size as epsilon, and is given standard normal priors (i.e. epsilon_raw ~ normal(0,1)). On Sunday, November 1, 2015 at 12:28:41 AM UTC+2, Colin Rust wrote:
> The following came up in an EVT (Extreme Value Theory) analysis of data on extreme geomagnetic storms.  These matter because a really extreme storm could fry a lot of telecom, etc.  So it's helpful to have an estimate of how the likelihood of storms of various magnitudes.
>
> Basically you have a data set (in this case with 67 points), and you know/believe the true distribution is drawn from a two parameter family (in this case Generalized Pareto).  You want to estimate the probability of an event above some extreme cutoff C, which is more that any point in your data set.  How do you go about this?
>
> 1. One approach would be to fit the ML distribution in the family and use that. This gives a point estimate of the probability P(X>C).
> 2. #1 can be extended using bootstrapping: Draw from the data set with replacement a bunch of samples of the same size (67 points).  From this, you can infer a distribution for the probability P(X>C) around the point estimate from #1.
>
> That (#1 and #2) exactly what David Roodman does here:
>
> http://blog.givewell.org/2015/07/13/geomagnetic-storms-using-extreme-value-theory-to-gauge-the-risk/
>
> (I also posted in the comments there.)
>
> That approach generated some weird results.  In particular, for some smaller cutoffs D that actually are reached in the data, it assigns non-zero probability to P(X>D) being 0 (hope that's not too confusing).
>
> So I was wondering if there's a better way than the bootstrap:  Instead assign a prior to the two parameter family of distributions (but what prior?).  Then, using the data, compute a posterior density over the two parameter family.  From there, you can then infer a distribution for P(X>C).
>
> Any thoughts appreciated. This may all be a little confusing with densities on densities so to speak, but hopefully it makes sense.
>

messages.body_plain:
Ther'es not a lot of room for improvement in a simple
regression.  It might help to give beta a tighter prior
and sigma_a and sigma_epsilon reasonable priors (at least
weakly informative).  But if you have that much data,
it's not likely to matter.

But what you probably want to do is go away from the
characterization of overdispersion with that vector of
epsilons and use a compound distribution like the
negative binomial.

- Bob

Andrew and Bob,

thank you a lot. I'm really new to this and I'm not sure about many parts of my code.

Bob,

x is not only the justice parameter, but this justice in a certain term. Therefore, for x_j_t, there is a x_j_{t-1}. I am not sure how to implement these in Stan. The problem is even worse because justices don't share the same number of terms, i. e., justice i might be deciding for 5 terms and justice j, for 10 terms. What I did: I mapped justice and term to a par, that's why I called par[i] in my model. For the same reason, I don't know even how to vectorize this in Stan.

npar is the number of pars I just defined. Suppose there is 3 justices (njus = 3): the first one served for 5 terms, the second, 4 terms, and the last, 7 terms. Thus there is njus=3 and npar=5+4+7=16.

Andrew,

Thanks for your suggestions. I will rewrite the code. I'm not sure if the second one is clear to me. Could you elaborate more?

G.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks.  I didn't realize it had a time series inside.  We're
working on IRT models a lot these days and I want to use this
one as an example of the differences with ideal-point models.

Here's what I came up with from the original paper, coded
in "long form" or "database form" or like a data frame in R.
I wasn't clear from skimming the model section of the paper what
priors were being used for alpha and beta and theta in the first
term --- I'd be inclined to make the model hierarchical.

What you'd need to do is actually set some of the theta values
by hand and let the other ones float.  You do that by defining
smaller vectors of the ones that float and then constructing ones
together that don't.  But hwy set all the justices in term 0?  Do
you really want Scalia and Thomas to both have position 2.5 in term 0?
And by term 0 did you mean term 1 if we're numbering from 1?  I got
a bit lost between yours and Martin and Quinn's notation.  I tried
to stick to theirs below.

/**
 *  Martin and Quinn (2002) Dynamic Ideal Point Estimation via
 *  Markov Chain Monte Carlo for the U.S. Supreme Court, 1953--1999.
 *
 *  Model section of paper is silent on fixed (?) priors for params.
 */
data {
  int<lower=0> T;                 // number of terms
  int<lower=0> J;                 // number of justices
  int<lower=0> K;                 // total number of cases

  int<lower=0> N;                 // num votes
  int<lower=1> tt[N];             // term for vote n
  int<lower=1> jj[N];             // justice for vote n
  int<lower=1> kk[N];             // case for vote n
  int<lower=0, upper=1> z[N];     // vote (yea = 1, nay = 0)

  vector[J] theta0;               // prior mean (M&Q: mu0)
  vector<lower=0>[J] delta0;      // initial t sd (M&Q: sqrt of C[0,])
  vector<lower=0>[J] delta[T-1];  // "evolution sd"  (M&Q: sqrt of Delta[t,j])
  vector[2] b0;                   // prior mean for pos and discrim
  cov_matrix[2] B0;               // prior covar for pos and discrim
}
parameters {
  vector[2] alpha_beta[K];        // position and discrim of case k
  vector[J] theta[T];             // position in term t of justice j
}
model {
  for (n in 1:N)
    z[n] ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha_beta[kk[n], 1]
                           + alpha_beta[kk[n], 2] * theta[tt[n], jj[n]]);

  alpha_beta ~ multi_normal(b0, B0);

  theta[1] ~ normal(theta0, delta0);
  for (t in 2:T)
    theta[t] ~ normal(theta[t - 1], delta[t - 1]);
}

If you get this working, can you send it back to us?  Or even better,
write it up in knitr as a case study?  We're about to start publishing
them on our web site for example models.  Sort of like the BUGS examples,
only new ones with a bit more description.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Bob,

Thanks a lot for your help.

Actually Martin and Quinn implemented the model in C++, so they started the terms with 0. As long as I'm using R, I decided to start with 1.

I'd be glad to write a case study in knitr.  I'm putting effort in implementing a lot of political science models in Stan, so I'll let you know.

Thanks.

On Mon, Nov 2, 2015 at 11:00 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> Thanks.  I didn't realize it had a time series inside.  We're
> working on IRT models a lot these days and I want to use this
> one as an example of the differences with ideal-point models.
>
> Here's what I came up with from the original paper, coded
> in "long form" or "database form" or like a data frame in R.
> I wasn't clear from skimming the model section of the paper what
> priors were being used for alpha and beta and theta in the first
> term --- I'd be inclined to make the model hierarchical.
>
> What you'd need to do is actually set some of the theta values
> by hand and let the other ones float.  You do that by defining
> smaller vectors of the ones that float and then constructing ones
> together that don't.  But hwy set all the justices in term 0?  Do
> you really want Scalia and Thomas to both have position 2.5 in term 0?
> And by term 0 did you mean term 1 if we're numbering from 1?  I got
> a bit lost between yours and Martin and Quinn's notation.  I tried
> to stick to theirs below.
>
>
> /**
>  *  Martin and Quinn (2002) Dynamic Ideal Point Estimation via
>  *  Markov Chain Monte Carlo for the U.S. Supreme Court, 1953--1999.
>  *
>  *  Model section of paper is silent on fixed (?) priors for params.
>  */
> data {
>   int<lower=0> T;                 // number of terms
>   int<lower=0> J;                 // number of justices
>   int<lower=0> K;                 // total number of cases
>
>   int<lower=0> N;                 // num votes
>   int<lower=1> tt[N];             // term for vote n
>   int<lower=1> jj[N];             // justice for vote n
>   int<lower=1> kk[N];             // case for vote n
>   int<lower=0, upper=1> z[N];     // vote (yea = 1, nay = 0)
>
>   vector[J] theta0;               // prior mean (M&Q: mu0)
>   vector<lower=0>[J] delta0;      // initial t sd (M&Q: sqrt of C[0,])
>   vector<lower=0>[J] delta[T-1];  // "evolution sd"  (M&Q: sqrt of Delta[t,j])
>   vector[2] b0;                   // prior mean for pos and discrim
>   cov_matrix[2] B0;               // prior covar for pos and discrim
> }
> parameters {
>   vector[2] alpha_beta[K];        // position and discrim of case k
>   vector[J] theta[T];             // position in term t of justice j
> }
> model {
>   for (n in 1:N)
>     z[n] ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha_beta[kk[n], 1]
>                            + alpha_beta[kk[n], 2] * theta[tt[n], jj[n]]);
>
>   alpha_beta ~ multi_normal(b0, B0);
>
>   theta[1] ~ normal(theta0, delta0);
>   for (t in 2:T)
>     theta[t] ~ normal(theta[t - 1], delta[t - 1]);
> }
>
>
> If you get this working, can you send it back to us?  Or even better,
> write it up in knitr as a case study?  We're about to start publishing
> them on our web site for example models.  Sort of like the BUGS examples,
> only new ones with a bit more description.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Nov 2, 2015, at 7:45 PM, Guilherme Jardim Duarte <gjardi...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Andrew and Bob,
> >
> > thank you a lot. I'm really new to this and I'm not sure about many parts of my code.
> >
> > Bob,
> >
> > x is not only the justice parameter, but this justice in a certain term. Therefore, for x_j_t, there is a x_j_{t-1}. I am not sure how to implement these in Stan. The problem is even worse because justices don't share the same number of terms, i. e., justice i might be deciding for 5 terms and justice j, for 10 terms. What I did: I mapped justice and term to a par, that's why I called par[i] in my model. For the same reason, I don't know even how to vectorize this in Stan.
> >
> > npar is the number of pars I just defined. Suppose there is 3 justices (njus = 3): the first one served for 5 terms, the second, 4 terms, and the last, 7 terms. Thus there is njus=3 and npar=5+4+7=16.
> >
> >
> > Andrew,
> >
> > Thanks for your suggestions. I will rewrite the code. I'm not sure if the second one is clear to me. Could you elaborate more?

> >
> >

> > >> On Nov 2, 2015, at 5:56 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> > >>
> > >> Hi, buncha things going on here, including:
> > >> 1.  Don’t plan to run 10^5 iterations.  If your model is making sense, 1000 should be a reasonable number.
> > >> 2.  If you’re using normal(1, .01) priors, you’ll have to specify the init in that range.  But do you really want to be specifying normal(1, .01) priors?  I suspect it’s better to just input these numbers as data.

ELBO itself is stochastic (noisy). therefore, taking samples from the
iteration with the best ELBO may not be reliable at all.

cheers

Hi Shuaiqi,

That's strange. It doesn't make sense for

rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

to be masked from Rcpp. Those lines are printed as part of RStan's package startup message, advising people that it can be useful to set those options if their system allows it.

Masking happens because a function/object in one package has the same name as one in a different package that's already loaded, so that when the second package is loaded it "masks" the function in the first package. Perhaps the message about masking is getting intertwined with the package startup message. I would guess that there's more text that gets printed to the console when this is happening. If so, can you share the full text of all the messages printed when this happens?

Thanks,

Jonah

thanks for your message. i think your understanding is spot on.

there is unfortunately no direct way of accessing Sigma = L^T L at the moment. the reason for this is that the normal approximation is in the unconstrained (transformed) space, and not in the original latent variable space. so Sigma is not of interest to the typical ADVI user.

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I am wondering if a discontinuity in the ODE system function is fine? My situation: I have a so-called lag-time PK model. This means that a concentration of exactly 0 is in the main cmt as long as 0 < t < t_lag . For t>=t_lag the PK concentration is non-zero.

First, I wanted to integrate from t=0 to t_lag and then integrate with matching initial values from t=t_lag to all time-points I am interested in, but then I noticed that the integrate_ode call does not allow t0 to be a parameter which would be my case here.

However, nothing seems to stop me from having an if-statement inside the ODE system functor, i.e. something like

function_being_integrated:

if(t < t_lag)
  return(0)
else
 calculate me

It feels strange that the above should work, but this would put all work to the integrator to deal with the discontinuity. I would much prefer to handle the discontinuity myself by step-wise integration, but this is not possible. Any thoughts?

Many thanks!

Best,
Sebastian

Dear all,

thanks to the help provided in this group, my model is now finally
converging properly.
In the end I re-parametrized 6 of the 7 group-level parameters with the
non-central form and roughly scaled them into similar ranges. For one
parameter this resulted in problems, so I left this one with in the
original version. Furthermore, I added some slightly(?) informative
priors for the group level parameters.

Here are diagnostics plots of ALL the parameters on all levels.

http://homepages.uni-paderborn.de/jeti/diag/

I think everything looks fine, doesn't it? Somewhere there is a bi-modal
posterior on the subject level, but I don't think this is any problem in
principle.

I have an intuition that a little bit of prior information goes a long way—that is, using soft constraints to knock out truly unreasonable values will have payoff throughout the analysis because of near-collinearity and similar issues. But N(0,10) is too weak to really regularize.

messages.subject: Bayesian hierarchical model: Unexpected strong shrinkage
messages.subject_clean: Bayesian hierarchical model: Unexpected strong shrinkage
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan users,

I am currently working on estimating effects (let's say, of a genetic variant) in various subgroups (e.g.  ethnicity, regions, or disease, with > 15 groups)  using a Bayesian hierarchical model with uninformative priors:

\begin{align}
  y_i      &\sim N(\theta_i, \sigma_i^2)\\
  \theta_i &\sim N(\mu, \tau^2) \\
  \sigma_i &\sim cauchy(0, 2 \times range_y) \\
  \mu      &\sim N(0, \tau^2) \\
  \tau     &= 100
\end{align}

I am trying to understand some unexpected results, which lead to extreme shrinkage across all subgroups compared to a fully stratified analysis in a specific dataset, giving very similar estimates and very similar credible intervals.

My current interpretation is that there a no differential effects/heterogeneity in the subgroups (e.g. Isquared~6%), and, therefore, the results are shrunken to the same estimate, comparable to a fixed effects model. However, I wonder why the credible intervals are of similar size, because the sample sizes and standard errors vary considerably in the fully stratified analysis. The variances of the prior distributions are large enough, so even larger values do not seem to affect the estimates or credible intervals.

My R/Stan code seems to be ok, since the results for the 8schools data set match other publications (Gelman, 2014, BDA3). However, in the 8schools results, heterogeneity is absent (Isquared=0%), but the shrinkage is much weaker (moderate) compared to the other model described above.

My questions:

1) What are factors influencing shrinkage (priors, overall effect size, number of subgroups, ..) which could explain these findings?
2) Are there criteria to evaluate whether the observed shrinkage is adequate?

3) Are there situations/data where a Bayesian hierarchical (shrinkage) model is not recommended?

Any comments are welcome!

Thanks in advance,

Wilmar

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Complex hierarchical model --- finally converging
messages.body_plain:
“Noninformative” and “conservative” are loaded terms with little formal
meaning, so you’re probably not going to get a particularly satisfactory
answer.  When you model you have to make assumptions, whether
it be in the form of the likelihood and the prior (the hierarchical structure)
or the hyperpriors.  The best you can really judge is whether or not those
assumptions are qualitatively consistent with the given data which requires
doing posterior predictive checks.

Andrew is just saying that O(10) is probably still extreme if you have
standardized all of your data so that your random effects should be O(1).
Tightening the prior will improve your posterior inferences provided that
you don’t tighten it so far that you start introducing tension with the data.

> > I have an intuition that a little bit of prior information goes a long way—that is, using soft constraints to knock out truly unreasonable values will have payoff throughout the analysis because of near-collinearity and similar issues.  The key is to knock out the unreasonable things.  So if you have a parameter that really can’t be more than 1 or less than -1, then N(0,1) is conservative but can do the job. logy_a <- rnorm(A, mean = 0, sd = 0.05)

The line above is to generate the input data for STAN model.

logy_a ~ normal(X_a, 0.5);
The line above in STAN is the data model, where I assume that logy_a follows an AR(1). X_a is the parameter vector that I want to estimate. As you mentioned, yes, I didn't generate logy_a by AR(1). The AR(1) process is coded in STAN model code. What I want to do is to make logy_a resemble some real-life data on log scale. I don't see the necessity of generating input data logy_a in R using AR(1) process. Whatever the underlying distribution it has, the chains should at least move around instead of staying at the exact same value.

Regards,
CFQ

messages.subject: Re: Possible to get a multivariate gamma density in STAN?
messages.subject_clean: Possible to get a multivariate gamma density in STAN?
messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, November 4, 2015 at 10:02:38 AM UTC-5, Royce Anders wrote:
> Would it be possible to get a multivariate gamma density in STAN?

Coding-wise, it would not be difficult at all to copy what we have for the Wishart distribution and modifying it slightly for the multivariate gamma. The problem is finding someone who is sufficiently motivated to do it because in order to put it into Stan it would also have to be tested at least as much as the Wishart distribution, documented, complimented with a function to draw from the multivariate gamma, etc. And that is all pretty tedious to do for a distribution that is not widely used and is not likely to lead to efficient sampling in Stan unless X were data.

If you are that motivated, then we can help you jump through the hoops involved when adding new functions to Stan. But if you are not so motivated, it is pretty easy to write that log density as a user-defined Stan function within a Stan program. And depending on what special case (diagonal scale matrix, etc.) you might be interested in, it may actually run faster than would a general implementation in the Stan Math Library.

Ben

We obviously need more specialized matrix operations in
the math library.  We've been kicking around the idea of
having various specializations, but the syntax is going to
be ugly.  Things like multiply_lower_triangular(matrix, real)
and multiple_lower_triangular(matrix, vector) and so on.
Plus all the positive-definite versions, and the symmetric
versions, multiply_symmetric(...), ...  I don't see how we
can overload the basic operations the way things are written now,
because run-time typing is just int / real / matrix / vector / row vector
and we don't have basic types for type inference for the triangular
and symmetric and other types of matrices we might want.

We could also add new data types the same way we added Cholesky.
That's not too hard to do --- Marcus managed to add one without
much help, but then he's a very skilled coder, so others' mileage
may vary.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Complex hierarchical model --- finally converging
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

OK, I should be able to select tighter normal priors for the means. But how about the gamma priors on the standard deviations? Any hints on how to set them?  Up to now I have been adjusting shape and rate until I thought it looks visually OK. But maybe you or someone has hints how to better set them if I have some rough expectancy for them?

Thanks and best regards
Jan

Sent from Samsung tablet.

-------- Original message --------
From: Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com>
Date:04/11/2015 14:06 (GMT+01:00)
To: stan-...@googlegroups.com
Subject: Re: [stan-users] Complex hierarchical model --- finally converging

“Noninformative” and “conservative” are loaded terms with little formal
meaning, so you’re probably not going to get a particularly satisfactory
answer.  When you model you have to make assumptions, whether
it be in the form of the likelihood and the prior (the hierarchical structure)
or the hyperpriors.  The best you can really judge is whether or not those
assumptions are qualitatively consistent with the given data which requires
doing posterior predictive checks.

Andrew is just saying that O(10) is probably still extreme if you have
standardized all of your data so that your random effects should be O(1).
Tightening the prior will improve your posterior inferences provided that
you don’t tighten it so far that you start introducing tension with the data.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] "pow" still in manual
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] "pow" still in manual
messages.body_plain:
If anyone has an issue with the manual, please report on
the issue tracker.  There's always a "next manual" issue named
after current release++.  Here's the current one for 2.8.0++:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1617

The models need a complete overhaul as our default advice on
priors, etc., has changed pretty thoroughly.  There are going to be even
bigger changes after I add the indexing.  We also don't use the nice
log_mix functions in mixture models.  I believe there may even be
some of those interval priors.

This is why there's a quadratic cost over the long run for adding
new material, including what look like simple examples.  See:

 http://andrewgelman.com/2013/11/04/joel-on-shlemiel-the-painter-unknown-unknowns/

The short version is that every example we add needs to be updated when we change
Stan (e.g., add sliced indexing, ^ operator) or when we change advice (e.g.,
on priors).

We even have examples in our repos with no vectorization and with
inv_gamma(0.001,0.001) priors!  We continually get people volunteering
to fix them all, but nobody lasts past more than one or two.
I suppose it's just not very glamorous or rewarding work.

- Bob

I narrowed this down to something to do with the large number of stored samples being recorded - I had lots of n ~ 20,000 vectors in the transformed parameters block and the generated quantities block that were being recorded.  Putting these in a local block (ie not saving their values) massively cut down on the initialisation time.

I guess this might be something to do with memory allocation, although the total memory allocation only ends up being 2 GB or so.  No idea why it would take an hour to allocate 2 GB of memory.

messages.subject: Re: New wiener distribution estimating parameters strangely from RWiener package
messages.subject_clean: New wiener distribution estimating parameters strangely from RWiener package
messages.body_plain:
I was able to actually recover the parameters in STAN generated from the RWiener package. It turns out I made a dumb mistake when indexing accuracy for the wiener likelihood. Just uploading correct code here just in case.

# install these packages if not already installed, run:
#    install.packages(c("rstan", "loo", "RWiener"))
library(rstan) # need to load namespace due to Rcpp dependencies

# for running multiple chains in parallel, uncomment next two lines
#rstan::rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
#options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

# wiener parameters to try and estimate in STAN
a <- 3
t <- 0.25
b <- 0.33
v <- 1
n <- 50

# random RT values from RWiener package using parameters from above
rt <- RWiener::rwiener(

    n = n,
    alpha = a,
    tau = t,
    beta = b,
    delta = v
)

# make stan data list
stan_data <- list(rt = rt$q,
                  acc = ifelse(rt[, "resp"] == "upper", 1, 0),
                  n = nrow(rt),

                  min_t = min(rt$q),
                  max_t = max(rt$q))

# number of chains to run

n_chains <- 3

# use initial values from above weiner parameters

stan_inits <- lapply(1:n_chains, function(i) {
    list(
        a = a,
        t = t,
        v = v,
        b = b
    )
})

# STAN model code

stan_model <-
"
data {
    int<lower=1>                n;
    vector[n]                   rt;
    vector<lower=0,upper=1>[n]  acc;
    real<lower=0>               min_t;

    real<lower=0>               max_t;
}
parameters {
    real<lower=0,upper=100>          a; // speed-acc tradeoff / boundary width
    real<lower=0.1,upper=min_t>      t; // motor latency / non-decision time
    real<lower=-max_t,upper=max_t>   v; // processing speed / drift rate
    real<lower=0,upper=1>            b; // response bias / boundary bias
}
model {
    a ~ gamma(0.75, 0.25);
    v ~ normal(0, max_t/3);
    b ~ beta(1.25, 1.25);
    // implied: t ~ uniform(0.1, mininum RT)

    // likelihood
    for (i in 1:n) {

        if (acc[i] == 1) {

            rt[i] ~ wiener(a, t, b, v);    // upper bound
        } else {

            rt[i] ~ wiener(a, t, 1 - b, -1 * v); // lower bound

        }
    }
}
generated quantities {
    vector[n] log_lik;

    for (i in 1:n) {

        if (acc[i] == 1) { // upper boundary

            log_lik[i] <- wiener_log(rt[i], a, t, b, v);

        } else {           // lower boundary
            log_lik[i] <- wiener_log(rt[i], a, t, 1 - b, -1 * v);
        }
    }
}
"

# Fit STAN model ----------------------------------------------------------

stan_fit <-
    rstan::stan(

        model_name = "diffusion_test",

# function to plot distributions from RWiener

plot_rwiener <- function(rt) {
    rt_u <- rt$q[rt$resp == "upper"]
    rt_l <- rt$q[rt$resp == "lower"]

    xlim <- max(c(rt_u, rt_l))
    rt_seq <- seq(0, xlim, .005)

    d_rt_u <-

        RWiener::dwiener(rt_seq, a, t, b, v, resp = rep("upper", length(rt_seq)))
    d_rt_l <-
        RWiener::dwiener(rt_seq, a, t, b, v, resp = rep("lower", length(rt_seq)))

    ylim <- max(c(d_rt_u, d_rt_l))

    par(mfrow = c(3, 1))

    plot(
        x = rt_seq,
        y = d_rt_u,
        type = "l",
        xlim = c(0, xlim),
        ylim = c(-ylim, ylim),
        main = "Density of upper/lower responses",
        ylab = "density",
        xlab = "quantile",
        col = "green"
    )

    lines(x = rt_seq, y = -d_rt_l, col = "red")

    xbrks <- seq(0, xlim, length.out = 30)

    hist(
        rt_u,
        freq = FALSE,
        breaks = xbrks,
        xlim = c(0, xlim),
        ylim = c(0, ylim * 2),
        main = "upper",
        xlab = paste("N =", length(rt_u))
    )

    hist(
        rt_l,
        freq = FALSE,
        breaks = xbrks,
        xlim = c(0, xlim),
        ylim = c(0, ylim * 2),
        main = "lower",
        xlab = paste("N =", length(rt_l))
    )
}

plot_rwiener(rt)

Hi Bob,

Thanks for your response and for outlining the major issues with my model. I apologize for my delay in reverting to you - I am undertaking fieldwork in a remote location in India and have very limited connectivity of any sort.

​To
answer
​​
your questions:

1. I used the Stan manual and online examples for constructing negative binomial models
​.​

2. The idea to jointly model the probability distributions comes from a publication that implemented this method using INLA in R.

​I have a couple of more questions in ​response to your suggestions:

​1. Can I define seed2 as a vector instead and use the ​generated quantities option to determine the values of seed2 from the distribution that describes it? I couldn't determine a way to draw random values from a prescribed distribution in Stan, as can be done in R.

2. Or, could I put the main response within the loop that computes seed2, writing it as:

​

 for(i in 1:N){
>     lamda[i] ~ lognormal(seed[i], sigma);
>     seed2[i] ~ neg_binomial_2(lamda[i], phisd);

>     sdl[i] ~ neg_binomial_2_log(exp(alpha)*seed2[i]^beta, phisdl);
       }
I had previously written it as this, but that was throwing errors too.

Thanks,
Meghna

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

May I ask what you read before you tried to write this
model?  The reason I ask is that the two problems in your
code are quite common and we'd like to be able to more
clearly formulate the issues.

Issue 1.

The variables in Stan need to be declared with constraints
so that any value satisfying the constraints has finite
log density.  So when you have a parameter declared
as

>   real sigma;

and a sampling statement

>   sigma ~ uniform(0,10);

you produce a problem where sigma < 0 or sigma > 10 satsify
the declared constraints (there aren't any).

If you insist on this prior, you need to declare

  real<lower=0, upper=10> sigma;

and similarly for the other parameters.

Issue 2.

You are using the local variable seed2 before it is defined:

  int seed2[N];
  ...
    seed2[i] ~ neg_binomial_2(lamda[i], phisd);

Stan doesn't work like BUGS --- this just increments the posterior
log density.  In BUGS, it defines an edge in a directed graphical
model.

I think the only solution is to marginalize seed2 out of your
model.  I'm not sure how a compound negative binomial works.  You're
giving your model a double-dose of overdispersion.

Issue 3.

You can't raise an array to a power, so seed2^beta is going to
be ill-formed as well.  The legal signatures are defined in the
index to the manual.

- Bob

- Bob

> On Nov 4, 2015, at 7:30 PM, Joseph Burling <joseph...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I was able to actually recover the parameters in STAN generated from the RWiener package. It turns out I made a dumb mistake when indexing accuracy for the wiener likelihood. Just uploading correct code here just in case.
>
> # install these packages if not already installed, run:
> #    install.packages(c("rstan", "loo", "RWiener"))
> library(rstan) # need to load namespace due to Rcpp dependencies
>
> # for running multiple chains in parallel, uncomment next two lines
> #rstan::rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
> #options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
>
> # wiener parameters to try and estimate in STAN
> a <- 3
> t <- 0.25
> b <- 0.33
> v <- 1
> n <- 50
>
> # random RT values from RWiener package using parameters from above
> rt <- RWiener::rwiener(
>     n = n,
>     alpha = a,
>     tau = t,
>     beta = b,
>     delta = v
> )
>
> # make stan data list
> stan_data <- list(rt = rt$q,
>                   acc = ifelse(rt[, "resp"] == "upper", 1, 0),
>                   n = nrow(rt),
>                   min_t = min(rt$q),
>                   max_t = max(rt$q))
>
> # number of chains to run
> n_chains <- 3
>
> # use initial values from above weiner parameters
> stan_inits <- lapply(1:n_chains, function(i) {
>     list(
>         a = a,
>         t = t,
>         v = v,
>         b = b
>     )
> })
>
> # STAN model code
> stan_model <-
> "
> data {
>     int<lower=1>                n;
>     vector[n]                   rt;
>     vector<lower=0,upper=1>[n]  acc;
>     real<lower=0>               min_t;
>     real<lower=0>               max_t;
> }
> parameters {
>     real<lower=0,upper=100>          a; // speed-acc tradeoff / boundary width
>     real<lower=0.1,upper=min_t>      t; // motor latency / non-decision time
>     real<lower=-max_t,upper=max_t>   v; // processing speed / drift rate
>     real<lower=0,upper=1>            b; // response bias / boundary bias
> }
> model {
>     a ~ gamma(0.75, 0.25);
>     v ~ normal(0, max_t/3);
>     b ~ beta(1.25, 1.25);
>     // implied: t ~ uniform(0.1, mininum RT)
>
>     // likelihood
>     for (i in 1:n) {
>         if (acc[i] == 1) {
>             rt[i] ~ wiener(a, t, b, v);    // upper bound
>         } else {
>             rt[i] ~ wiener(a, t, 1 - b, -1 * v); // lower bound
>         }
>     }
> }
> generated quantities {
>     vector[n] log_lik;
>
>     for (i in 1:n) {
>         if (acc[i] == 1) { // upper boundary
>             log_lik[i] <- wiener_log(rt[i], a, t, b, v);
>         } else {           // lower boundary
>             log_lik[i] <- wiener_log(rt[i], a, t, 1 - b, -1 * v);
>         }
>     }
> }
> "
>
> # Fit STAN model ----------------------------------------------------------
>
> stan_fit <-
>     rstan::stan(
>         model_name = "diffusion_test",
>         model_code = stan_model,
>         data = stan_data,
>         init = stan_inits,
>         chains = n_chains,
>         iter = n_chains * 1000
>     )
>
> # print stan model parameters
> print(stan_fit)
>
> # print elpd_loo, expected log-prob density of leave-one-out cross validation with importance sampling
> print(loo::loo(loo::extract_log_lik(stan_fit)), digits = 3)
>
> # print log likelihood from RWiener package
> print(RWiener::wiener_likelihood(c(a,t,b,v), rt))

messages.body_plain:
Is there a reproducible example?  This is an RStan (or PyStan)
issue --- there's no preallocation in CmdStan.

- Bob

> On Nov 4, 2015, at 6:46 PM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I narrowed this down to something to do with the large number of stored samples being recorded - I had lots of n ~ 20,000 vectors in the transformed parameters block and the generated quantities block that were being recorded.  Putting these in a local block (ie not saving their values) massively cut down on the initialisation time.
>
> I guess this might be something to do with memory allocation, although the total memory allocation only ends up being 2 GB or so.  No idea why it would take an hour to allocate 2 GB of memory.
>
>
> On Thursday, 29 October 2015 04:55:17 UTC+11, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> If you have those interval constraints on parameters, remember
> the default inits are around the middle of the range, which can
> be very problematic.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Oct 27, 2015, at 10:07 PM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I've checked with a print() statement that it's not the transformed parameters block.
> >
> > The parameter constraints should be easily satisfied (my parameters are all defined as reals or real<lower=0)s), but it's possible that the initial values produce infinities somewhere because I have a Poisson model with a bunch of exp terms all over the place (could be getting underflow or overflow somewhere...)
> >
> > Thanks for the suggestions - I will try to see if I can identify the problem through elimination.  I might try passing better inits in and seeing if that helps (at the moment I'm just going with the default)
> >
> >
> >
> > On Tuesday, 27 October 2015 03:09:52 UTC+11, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > It can do up to 100 initializations before giving up when
> > it can't find an initialization that works.  So the first
> > iteration can do 100 evaluations of the log density and
> > gradient even if it doesn't go anywhere.  Of course, it might
> > do 1000 evaluations in one iteration under default parameters, too --- depends on the
> > model and inits.   So you should see how many leapfrog steps
> > were done in that step.
> >
> > Also, make sure that every value of variables that satisfies
> > the declared constraints has finite log density in the model.
> > If not, init has to do a lot of guessing and then sampling can
> > devolve to a random walk because of boundary rejections.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> > > On Oct 26, 2015, at 3:05 AM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > I have refresh=1 in the call to Stan, so I see what's happening sample-by-sample - so I am seeing the first iteration.
> > >
> > > I do have a fair bit of stuff in the transformed data block, but it's basically just mapping input parameters into vectors or matrices for later use, and some standardisation of data (dividing by standard deviation etc).
> > >
> > > I don't have many initial parameter constraints - all my parameters are basically defined on (-infinity,infinity) or (0,infinity).  I have priors on everything.   My model does have exponential transformations of predictors though.... which might end up being rounded to infinity for poor initial starting choices.
> > >
> > > Could it be that the model is trying to generate parameters which give an infinity somewhere, and is then trying again lots of times until it gets something meaningful?
> > >
> > > Thanks
> > >
> > >
> > > On Monday, 26 October 2015 16:40:41 UTC+11, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > First, the data's read in and the transformed data block is
> > > executed and all constraints are validated.  That's about it.
> > >
> > > I believe RStan also allocates memory to store the draws
> > > at that point, the speed of which will depend on how
> > > you're running it.  Are you sure you're not also waiting
> > > for the first 10% of iterations?  The warmup iterations
> > > can be slow when they start adapting but haven't found
> > > the high probability mass volume of the posterior.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > > > On Oct 25, 2015, at 9:59 PM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Hi all,

> > > > I have a fairly complicated regression-type model which runs slowly but fine (500 iterations is a few hours). The model has N of about 20,000.

>
> I showed that when a drawn sigmaSquared value is > 20, the variance of the full conditional distribution for a0 takes a negative value, making it impossible to make another a0 draw.

The only way this would happen is if your joint distribution is
improper.

The warning you get from Stan is probably during warmup when it's
trying to find appropriate scales.  I'm not sure whether the current RStan
reports when the error occurs --- the behavior's changed recently because of
the number of complaints about too many warning messages on the fly.

You can try starting with a smaller initial
stepsize and higher target acceptance rate, which can help with numerical instability:

  control = list(stepsize=0.01, adapt_delta=0.99)

You can also make the model much more efficient with vectorization.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Suggestion for prior distribution of slope parameter when having a specific hypothesis on its value
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Suggestion for prior distribution of slope parameter when having a specific hypothesis on its value
messages.body_plain:
I don't understand what you mean by "first principles", because
if first principles say a value has to be 1.5, then you should just
set it to 1.5.

If I understand your literal question, namely test the hypothesis
that theta = 1.5, then the answer is 0 for a Bayesian, because

  Pr[theta = 1.5 | data] = 0

unless the prior or likelihood prohibit values other than 1.5.

You could estimate

  Pr[(1.5 - epsilon) < theta < (1.5 + epsilon) | data],

which should always be positive assuming the posterior has support
in an interval around theta.

The joy of Bayesian inference is that if the data constrains
theta to be very close to 1.5, then posterior inference will
take that into account without your having to make a hard
hypothesis-test type decision.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Possible to get a multivariate gamma density in STAN?
messages.body_plain:
There are two QR-decomposition functions (qr_Q, qr_R) for the two matrices.

It would be more efficient if we had a way to return both qr_Q and qr_R as
a single object --- we should probably have a function that just concatenates
one on top of the other, which would be easy to decompose back in the Stan code.
But we don't have that yet.

- Bob

> On Nov 5, 2015, at 6:36 AM, Royce Anders <ander...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
>
>

> >

> > Would it be possible to get a multivariate gamma density in STAN?
> >
> > Coding-wise, it would not be difficult at all to copy what we have for the Wishart distribution and modifying it slightly for the multivariate gamma. The problem is finding someone who is sufficiently motivated to do it because in order to put it into Stan it would also have to be tested at least as much as the Wishart distribution, documented, complimented with a function to draw from the multivariate gamma, etc.
>
> I think of the testing and API doc as part of the total "coding" process.
>
> > And that is all pretty tedious to do for a distribution that is not widely used and is not likely to lead to efficient sampling in Stan unless X were data.
> >
> > If you are that motivated, then we can help you jump through the hoops involved when adding new functions to Stan. But if you are not so motivated, it is pretty easy to write that log density as a user-defined Stan function within a Stan program. And depending on what special case (diagonal scale matrix, etc.) you might be interested in, it may actually run faster than would a general implementation in the Stan Math Library.
>

> I think indeed an interesting first step could be to try the log density as a user-defined Stan function. I'd be happy to report on it, and if the experiences pove worthwhile to implement it in STAN formally, I'd be happy to also help with its implementation.
>
> I took a try at a log density user-defined Stan function for the multivariate gamma, and according to Bob's comment below, I believe I got stuck due to limited matrix operations.
>
> I followed a technique based on Song (2000), in which one uses normal copula's, involving QR decomposition and solving the linear inverse problem of the QR decomposition, to estimate the density. I believe with this third step, is where I couldn't find such a function for STAN. According to your note here, perhaps I'm highly overcomplicating the calculation of this density, and I would be happy to receive help. I'm looking for the aka matrix gamma distribution, parameterized by  (shape, scale, E), where E is the symmetric correlation matrix.
>
> Otherwise, if there are simple STAN codes to easily get these R equivalents, I might be able to figure this out already:
> If E is a pxp symmetric correlation matrix, I would need the following STAN equivalents for this code in R:
> 1) The diagonal of qr(E)$qr      ## here $qr is a pxp matrix, in which the upper triangle is R and the lower is Q;      and
> 2) qr.solve(qr(E))         ## which solves the linear inverse problem, giving a pxp matrix.
>
> again maybe there is a much easier solution to calculating this density than what I've been looking at.

>
>
> We obviously need more specialized matrix operations in
> the math library.  We've been kicking around the idea of
> having various specializations, but the syntax is going to
> be ugly.  Things like multiply_lower_triangular(matrix, real)
> and multiple_lower_triangular(matrix, vector) and so on.
> Plus all the positive-definite versions, and the symmetric
> versions, multiply_symmetric(...), ...  I don't see how we
> can overload the basic operations the way things are written now,
> because run-time typing is just int / real / matrix / vector / row vector
> and we don't have basic types for type inference for the triangular
> and symmetric and other types of matrices we might want.
>
> We could also add new data types the same way we added Cholesky.
> That's not too hard to do --- Marcus managed to add one without
> much help, but then he's a very skilled coder, so others' mileage
> may vary.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Possible to get a multivariate gamma density in STAN?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Possible to get a multivariate gamma density in STAN?
messages.body_plain:
> According to your note here, perhaps I'm highly overcomplicating the calculation of this density, and I would be happy to receive help. I'm looking for the aka matrix gamma distribution, parameterized by  (shape, scale, E), where E is the symmetric correlation matrix.

This one, right?

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_gamma_distribution

Anything involving a QR decomposition is not going to be very efficient in Stan. The best way to do something like this would be to parameterize it in terms of the Cholesky factor, L, of Sigma = L * L'. So you get a log-PDF

(-2 * alpha) * log(det(L)) - (p * alpha) * log(beta)
- 0.25 * p * (p - 1) * sum(lgamma(alpha), ..., lgamma(alpha + 0.5 * (1 - p)))
+ (alpha - 0.5 * (p - 1)) * log(det(X)) - 1 / beta * trace( L^{-1}' * L^{-1} * X )
log(det(L)) is straightforward because it is the sum of the logarithms of the diagonal elements of L
if X is fixed then you can omit the term involving log(det(X)) or calculate it once in transformed data; if X is a parameter utilize Stan's log_determinant(X) function, which is more efficient than log(determinant(X))
Rewrite trace( L^{-1}' * L^{-1} * X ) as trace( L^{-1} * X * L^{-1}' )  by the cyclic permutation property and utilize Stan's trace_quad_form(L_inv_t, X) function for efficiency. This will require you compute L_inv_t = L^{-1}', which can be done efficiently utilizing Stan's transpose(mdivide_left_tri_low(L, I))
If you think of Sigma as a correlation matrix, then L needs to a parameter of type cholesky_factor_corr[p] and a good prior on L is lkj_corr_cholesky(1.0). If you think of Sigma as a covariance matrix, you will need to fix its trace, in which case a good choice for the vector of variances is a simplex. You can utilize Stan's diag_pre_multipy() function to multiply a diagonal matrix of standard deviations by the Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix to get a Cholesky factor of a covariance matrix.

By all means, use the expose_stan_functions() function in rstan to verify that your user-defined log-PDF returns the same number as whatever R implementation you have at your disposal.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
This is an issue with how RStan deals with environments.
You must have something non-numerical in your top-level environment
and RStan just converts everything.  So it's both inefficient
and unpredictable as written if you don't know what's going to be
in your envioronment.  I have no idea if this is fixable on the RStan
side so that it only looks for values in the model, but for now, that's
what happens.

To fix, you need to do one of

a.  make sure there's no extraneous non-numerical variables (and ideally no
other variables for efficiency) in the environment from which stan() is called, or

b.  explicitly specify the names of variables to read from the environment (all the
data variables), or

c.  provide the data as a named list.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Suggestion for prior distribution of slope parameter when having a specific hypothesis on its value
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Suggestion for prior distribution of slope parameter when having a specific hypothesis on its value
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I think the point is that when you have a parameter with a true value of 1.5 (say)  in the theoretical model, it won’t be exactly 1.5 when fit to data, because of measurement error and misspecification.  In your setting, one option is to just set b to 1.5 as data and then check the fit of your model using posterior predictive checks.
Another option is to give b a fairly strong prior, such as N(1.5, .5) which will pull the estimate toward your prior model.  Yet another approach is to set b to 1.5 and then add another parameter to capture model misspecification.

> On Nov 5, 2015, at 1:14 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> I don't understand what you mean by "first principles", because
> if first principles say a value has to be 1.5, then you should just
> set it to 1.5.
>
> If I understand your literal question, namely test the hypothesis
> that theta = 1.5, then the answer is 0 for a Bayesian, because
>
>  Pr[theta = 1.5 | data] = 0
>
> unless the prior or likelihood prohibit values other than 1.5.
>
> You could estimate
>
>  Pr[(1.5 - epsilon) < theta < (1.5 + epsilon) | data],
>
> which should always be positive assuming the posterior has support
> in an interval around theta.
>
> The joy of Bayesian inference is that if the data constrains
> theta to be very close to 1.5, then posterior inference will
> take that into account without your having to make a hard
> hypothesis-test type decision.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, November 5, 2015 at 5:31:23 PM UTC-5, dqsIJan Tünnermann wrote:
> Does anyone have a suggestion for how to find an intuition for the parameters of the gamma distribution? What I mean is, when I expect the parameter (a group standard deviation) around a certain value, how can I select a reasonable gamma prior for it?
>

curve(from=0, to=5, expr=dgamma(shape=2, rate=1, log=FALSE))

also, the wikipedia article on the gamma has expressions for the mean/median/variance which help.

Krzysztof

> Thanks and best regards
> Jan
>
> On 11/04/2015 09:42 PM, Jan Tünnermann wrote:
> > Hi Michael,
> >
> > OK, I should be able to select tighter normal priors for the means. But how about the gamma priors on the standard deviations? Any hints on how to set them?  Up to now I have been adjusting shape and rate until I thought it looks visually OK. But maybe you or someone has hints how to better set them if I have some rough expectancy for them?
> >
> > Thanks and best regards
> > Jan
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > Sent from Samsung tablet.
> >

> > To: stan-...@googlegroups.com
> > Subject: Re: [stan-users] Complex hierarchical model --- finally converging
> >
> > “Noninformative” and “conservative” are loaded terms with little formal
> > meaning, so you’re probably not going to get a particularly satisfactory
> > answer.  When you model you have to make assumptions, whether
> > it be in the form of the likelihood and the prior (the hierarchical structure)
> > or the hyperpriors.  The best you can really judge is whether or not those
> > assumptions are qualitatively consistent with the given data which requires
> > doing posterior predictive checks.
> >
> > Andrew is just saying that O(10) is probably still extreme if you have
> > standardized all of your data so that your random effects should be O(1).
> > Tightening the prior will improve your posterior inferences provided that
> > you don’t tighten it so far that you start introducing tension with the data.
> >
> > On Nov 4, 2015, at 7:51 AM, Jan Tünnermann <je...@mail.upb.de> wrote:
> >
> > > Dear Andrew,
> > >
> > > thanks for the reply. I'm not sure I understand. Is the problem that my priors are essentially flat over the relvant range?
> > > What would the mentioned payoff be (for example)?
> > >
> > > Many thanks and best regards
> > > Jan
> > >
> > > On 11/04/2015 03:05 AM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > > > I have an intuition that a little bit of prior information goes a long way—that is, using soft constraints to knock out truly unreasonable values will have payoff throughout the analysis because of near-collinearity and similar issues.  The key is to knock out the unreasonable things.  So if you have a parameter that really can’t be more than 1 or less than -1, then N(0,1) is conservative but can do the job.  But N(0,10) is too weak to really regularize.
> > > > A
> > > >
> > > > > On Nov 3, 2015, at 6:28 PM, Jan Tünnermann <je...@mail.upb.de> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > One thing remains where I am a bit unsure. I find it difficult to judge how informative the priors are. I would like to keep it pretty conservative, so I tried to only avoid extreme values. Furthermore, I have an experimental and one neutral control condition. I used priors (at least for the means) that reflect the neutral state (e.g., no shift effect, equally distributed weights, etc.) and are quite diffuse for both conditions.
> > > > >
> > > > > I plotted the posteriors for parameters from each condition together with a visualization of their common prior:
> > > > >
> > > > > http://homepages.uni-paderborn.de/jeti/priors/
> > > > >
> > > > > I'm very interested in your opinions regarding the informativeness of these priors? From what I see the data clearly dominate the distributions.
> > > > >
> > > > > And do you think using the "neutral" prior as described above for both conditions is a conservative choice? As I'm interested in the differences neutral-experimental, it could only reduce the detected effects.

Jan, rules of thumb:

1) rate is just 1/scale
2) mean ~ 1/rate when shape > 1, stick to shape = 2 unless you need a tighter tail on the high end
3) the mass for rates ~ 2 is mostly between zero and 2 or 3 * scale
4) the slope at zero is positive for shape > 1 (?) so essentially it weakly avoids that edge... not sure how this compares to half-cauchy with zero-bounded parameter

It would have been nice if all Stan distributions went either with scale or rate parameterization but....

Krzysztof

On Thursday, November 5, 2015 at 7:23:17 PM UTC-5, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
> It would have been nice if all Stan distributions went either with scale or rate parameterization but....

Well, we mostly went with BDA parameterizations which often followed Bayesian conventions and Bayesian conventions were usually designed to facilitate Gibbs sampling. And as we went along, we came to realize how important it is to establish a reasonable scale for parameters when using the default sampler in Stan. So, it probably would have been better to use scale parameterizations from the outset. But for priors on unknown quantities, it is typically a good idea to define a primitive in the parameters block whose prior entails scale = 1 = rate and than multiply that primitive by your prior scale inside the transformed parameters block to get the quantity that corresponds to the algebraic representation of the log-likelihood.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, November 5, 2015 at 10:45:39 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I don’t know, it’s just the way they always wrote it in the textbooks.  When I learned probability theory in 1981, my textbook had the exponential distribution and it was parameterized according to the rate parameter.  Nothing Bayesian about it, it’s just the convention.

I would agree that the frequentists had conventions about parameterizations prior to Gibbs sampling but, at least for maximum likelihood, the frequentists didn't have a frequentist justification for one parameterization over another due to the invariance property. Substantively, in the context of a duration model, it could either make sense to think of events occurring at some rate or to think about the mean of an exponential process.

But I don't think substantive reasons should be that relevant to how Stan parameterizes distributions because a user could just declare a rate parameter in the parameters block, specify an informative prior on the rate in the model block, and flip it over when putting into a likelihood that is parameterized in terms of scale (or vice versa). For technical reasons, it seems that HMC is more suited to scale (re)parameterizations, but those parameterizations tend to run counter to the parameterizations Bayesians were using for technical reasons when they were developing Gibbs samplers.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
   I’ve attempted to install and run MatlabStan (v. 2.7.0; cmdstan 2.8.0; operating system Mac OS X 10.10.5), but am unsuccessful for reasons I can’t figure out. Running, for example, the eight-schools example gives the following error:

Having a problem getting stan version.
This is likely a problem with Java running out of file descriptors
Trying again. [repeated 6 times]
Giving up.
Error using processManager/start (line 402)
Looks like command doesn't exist. Check spelling or path?
Error in processManager/set.command (line 212)
            self.start();
Error in processManager (line 179)
         self.command = p.Results.command;
Error in StanModel/stan_version (line 789)
         p = processManager('id','stanc version','command',command,...
Error in StanModel (line 194)
               ver = self.stan_version();
Error in stan (line 108)
   model = StanModel();
Error in school_test (line 27)
fit = stan('model_code',schools_code,'data',schools_dat);

This error & message seems very similar to an issue reported elsewhere, caused by MATLAB not using the appropriate libraries, using its own rather than those in /usr/lib .  See e.g. items 13-18 at https://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/newsreader/view_thread/162466, or http://sgpsproject.sourceforge.net/JavierVGomez/index.php/Solving_issues_with_GLIBCXX_and_libstdc%2B%2B . However, trying the solutions posted at these places does not work. (Essentially, many of the solutions involve setting the LD_PRELOAD variable to, for example, /usr/lib/libstdc++.so.6  to redirect to the proper libraries.)  I think this fails for me because in Mac OS X there is no LD_LIBRARY_PATH variable; the prior discussion of solutions is all for Unix. Also, I don't see libstdc++... in Matlab's binary directories, and don't know what other things I should be looking for. It’s very non-obvious (to me) how to direct Matlab to the proper libraries. (I tried “setenv('DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH', '/usr/lib’);” — this also fails. It is also, of course, possible that the problem is something completely different!

Has anyone used MatlabStan with OS X ? If so, is there some necessary step I’m missing?

(Running Stan from the command line, not through Matlab, works, by the way.)

Any thoughts are very much appreciated!

best wishes,

Raghu

PyStan 2.8.0.2 is available on PyPI. This releases contains a variety of
minor improvements. The Stan library used remains the same (2.8.0).

Highlights:

- Compiler optimization is turned on for model compilation.
- Specifying a subset of parameters (via the `pars` keyword) in sampling
  now works as expected.
- Python 3.5 support.

One important note about this release: PyStan 2.8.0.2 requires Cython
0.22 or higher (previously 0.19 or higher had been required). Cython's
support for interfacing with C++ code has improved tremendously in the
past year. Many bugs have been fixed.  Requiring Cython 0.22 means that
there need to be fewer bug workarounds in PyStan. Newer versions of
Python (3.5+) already require a higher version of Cython.

Download the latest version at

https://pypi.python.org/pypi/pystan

I can say with confidence that it's not the number of parameters as I'm working with a model that has about 13k parameters and it runs in about an hour.  The lack of indentation in your pasted code makes it hard to read but Z_ab should probably be re-parameterized (it's currently a t-distributed parameter, you can keep the distribution but create it using a transformed parameter---it's been discussed on list) you also have a state-space AR model which there was some talk about working better with a non-centered parameterization. > Hi all,
>
> I have troubles of fitting this model (at the end of this post) effectively. The model has 1010 parameters (my actual model has 8000+ parameters...). The parameters are nicely estimated when I set a specific seed number in function sampling(). If I change to any other seed number or do not specify it, the chains do not move at all even if I set adapt_delta extremely close to 1. As shown in the sampling() function below, I only reset adapt_deta and max_treedepth under "control", and all the rest arguments under "control" are kept at their default values.
>
> My question is: which arguments can I change in order to improve the sampler performance (i.e. make the chains move)? In the model below, luckily I've found a certain seed number which makes the sampler works fine. But this is after I've run the model for so many times. My actual model has a much larger number of parameters, and I guess it will take me forever to find the right seed number for my actual model... I've made adapt_delta as large as I can, but it didn't help much.
> Any suggestions/tips?? Or did I wrote my model in such a way that STAN is not able to run efficiently? Thanks.
>
> ## test the AR(1) model ##
> library(rstan)
> A <- 20
> B <- 25
> E <- 5
> N <- A * B
> a_n <- rep(1:A, each = B)
> b_n <- rep(1:B, times = A)
> e_n <- rep(E:1, each = N/E)
> pri_rho_lower <- 0
> pri_rho_upper <- 1
> pri_sigma_eps_lower <- 0
> pri_sigma_eps_upper <- 0.05
> pri_sigmas_lower <- 0
> pri_sigmas_upper <- 2
> pri_nu_lower <- 3
> pri_nu_upper <- 50
> X_lower <- log(0.5)
> X_upper <- log(2)
>
> set.seed(1234)
> logy <- rnorm(N, mean = 0, sd = 0.05)
>
> test_data <- list(A = A, B = B, N = N, E = E,
>                   logy = logy,
>                   a_n = a_n, b_n = b_n, e_n = e_n,
>                   X_lower = X_lower, X_upper = X_upper,
>                   pri_sigmas_lower = pri_sigmas_lower,
>                   pri_sigmas_upper = pri_sigmas_upper,
>                   pri_nu_lower = pri_nu_lower,
>                   pri_nu_upper = pri_nu_upper,
>                   pri_rho_lower = pri_rho_lower,
>                   pri_rho_upper = pri_rho_upper,
>                   pri_sigma_eps_lower = pri_sigma_eps_lower,
>                   pri_sigma_eps_upper = pri_sigma_eps_upper)
>
> test_model1 <- "
> data {
> int<lower=1> A;
> int<lower=1> B;
> int<lower=1> N;
> int<lower=1> E;
> int<lower=1, upper=A> a_n[N];
> int<lower=1, upper=B> b_n[N];
> int<lower=1, upper=E> e_n[N];
> real logy[N];
> real X_lower;
> real X_upper;
> real<lower=0> pri_rho_lower;
> real<lower=0> pri_rho_upper;
> real<lower=0> pri_sigma_eps_lower;
> real<lower=0> pri_sigma_eps_upper;
> real<lower=1> pri_nu_lower;
> real<lower=1> pri_nu_upper;
> real<lower=0> pri_sigmas_lower;
> real<lower=0> pri_sigmas_upper;
> }//end of data
>
> parameters {
> matrix[A,B] Z_ab;
> real<lower=pri_rho_lower, upper=pri_rho_upper> rho;
> real<lower=pri_sigma_eps_lower, upper=pri_sigma_eps_upper> sigma_eps;
> real<lower=pri_sigmas_lower, upper=0.05> sigma_e[E];
> real<lower=pri_nu_lower, upper=pri_nu_upper> nu;
> }//end of parameters
>
> transformed parameters {
> matrix<lower=X_lower, upper=X_upper>[A,B] X_ab;
> real<lower=0> sigma_eps_stat;
> sigma_eps_stat <- sqrt(sigma_eps^2 / (1 - rho^2));
>
> for (a in 1:A) {
> X_ab[a, 1] <- X_lower + inv_logit(sigma_eps_stat * Z_ab[a, 1]) * (X_upper - X_lower);
> for (b in 2:B) {
> X_ab[a, b] <- X_lower +
> inv_logit(rho * X_ab[a, b-1] + sigma_eps * Z_ab[a, b]) * (X_upper - X_lower);
> }//end of b loop
> }//end of a loop
> }//end of transformed parameters
>
> model {
> rho ~ uniform(pri_rho_lower, pri_rho_upper);
> sigma_eps ~ uniform(pri_sigma_eps_lower, pri_sigma_eps_upper);
> nu ~ uniform(pri_nu_lower, pri_nu_upper);
> sigma_e ~ uniform(pri_sigmas_lower, pri_sigmas_upper);
>
> for (a in 1:A)
> for (b in 1:B)
> Z_ab[a, b] ~ student_t(nu, 0, 1);
> // data model //
> for (n in 1:N) {
> logy[n] ~ normal(X_ab[a_n[n], b_n[n]], sqrt(0.05^2 + sigma_e[e_n[n]]^2));
> }//end of n loop
> }//end of model
> "
>
> fit_test1 <- sampling(
>   object = stan_model(model_code = test_model1),
>   data = test_data,
>   seed = 1973597442, #this seed works when A=20, B=25
>   control = list(
>     # adapt_gamma: default=0.05
>     adapt_gamma = 0.05,
>     # adapt_kappa: default=0.8
>     adapt_kappa = 0.8,
>     # adapt_t0: default=10
>     adapt_t0 = 10,
>     # adapt_init_buffer: default=75
>     adapt_init_buffer = 75,
>     # adapt_term_buffer: default=50
>     adapt_term_buffer = 50,
>     # adapt_window: default=25
>     adapt_window = 25,
>     # adapt_delta: target acceptance probability; default=0.8; max=0.9999999999999999444222
>     adapt_delta = 0.9999999999999999444222,
>     # max_treedepth: should increase if adapt_delta is high; default=10.
>     max_treedepth = 100),
>   iter = 1000, chains = n_chains, warmup = 2)
>
>
> ## trace plot
> traceplot(fit_test1,
>           par = c(dimnames(fit_test1)[[3]][sample(1:dim(fit_test1)[3], size = 4)],
>                   paste0("sigma_e", "[", 1:E, "]"),
>                   "rho", "sigma_eps", "nu"))

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for the very thorough and helpful responses all!! I will have a go at implementing the advice and return with news.

One quick thing to clarify if you please: in the general case, if one uses a user-defined distribution as a parameter prior; then instead of using, for example:

for(i in 1:nparams){
y[i] ~ dcustom_prior(a,b);
}

One would instead use

for(i in 1:nparams){
increment_log_prob(dcustom_prior(y[i],a,b));
}

?

On Thu, Nov 5, 2015 at 8:37 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > According to your note here, perhaps I'm highly overcomplicating the calculation of this density, and I would be happy to receive help. I'm looking for the aka matrix gamma distribution, parameterized by  (shape, scale, E), where E is the symmetric correlation matrix.
>
> This one, right?
>
> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_gamma_distribution
>
> Anything involving a QR decomposition is not going to be very efficient in Stan. The best way to do something like this would be to parameterize it in terms of the Cholesky factor, L, of Sigma = L * L'. So you get a log-PDF
>
> (-2 * alpha) * log(det(L)) - (p * alpha) * log(beta)
> - 0.25 * p * (p - 1) * sum(lgamma(alpha), ..., lgamma(alpha + 0.5 * (1 - p)))
> + (alpha - 0.5 * (p - 1)) * log(det(X)) - 1 / beta * trace( L^{-1}' * L^{-1} * X )
> log(det(L)) is straightforward because it is the sum of the logarithms of the diagonal elements of L
> if X is fixed then you can omit the term involving log(det(X)) or calculate it once in transformed data; if X is a parameter utilize Stan's log_determinant(X) function, which is more efficient than log(determinant(X))
> Rewrite trace( L^{-1}' * L^{-1} * X ) as trace( L^{-1} * X * L^{-1}' )  by the cyclic permutation property and utilize Stan's trace_quad_form(L_inv_t, X) function for efficiency. This will require you compute L_inv_t = L^{-1}', which can be done efficiently utilizing Stan's transpose(mdivide_left_tri_low(L, I))
> If you think of Sigma as a correlation matrix, then L needs to a parameter of type cholesky_factor_corr[p] and a good prior on L is lkj_corr_cholesky(1.0). If you think of Sigma as a covariance matrix, you will need to fix its trace, in which case a good choice for the vector of variances is a simplex. You can utilize Stan's diag_pre_multipy() function to multiply a diagonal matrix of standard deviations by the Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix to get a Cholesky factor of a covariance matrix.
>
> By all means, use the expose_stan_functions() function in rstan to verify that your user-defined log-PDF returns the same number as whatever R implementation you have at your disposal.
>
>
> Ben
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] STAN does not work well for models with large number of parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] STAN does not work well for models with large number of parameters
messages.body_plain:
Usually tightly constrained, non-unit-scaled parameters are
difficult:

  real<lower=pri_sigmas_lower, upper=0.05> sigma_e[E];

Warmup is going to need to find the scale to move sigma_e.

You don't need uniform distributions explicitly if the constraints
match.  And if the constraints don't match, you'll have bigger problems.
For instance, this is inconsistent:

  real<lower=pri_sigmas_lower, upper=0.05> sigma_e[E];

  ...

  sigma_e ~ uniform(pri_sigmas_lower, pri_sigmas_upper);

unless pri_sigmas_upper = 0.05. Every variable value that satisifies
the constraint should have support in the model (note that the converse
is not necessary).

You also have some implicit transforms, like

  logy[n] ~ normal(X_ab[a_n[n], b_n[n]], sqrt(0.05^2 + sigma_e[e_n[n]]^2));

where the .05^2 is going to be some tiny increment to sigma_e, which is
already bounded by pri_sigmas_lower.    I think it'd be easier to just put
the constraint you care about on sigma_e and then put a prior on the
constrained variable.

And finally some general advice:  work up to more complicated models with
simpler models to start.  Finally, this is going to be problematic numrically:

    adapt_delta = 0.9999999999999999444222,

Floating-point precision just isn't that high, so that number overflows to 1,
which requires every single state to be accepted, which is probably causing
a ridiculously small step size.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Dirichlet-multinomial GLM
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Dirichlet-multinomial GLM
messages.body_plain:
There are two approaches that would make sense.

1.  Actually do the implicit parameterization of the Dirichlet-multinomial
with the latent simplex variables and define theta to be a parameter and
use

paramters {
  simplex[K] theta[N];
  ...
model {
   theta[n] ~ dirichlet(alpha);
   y[n] ~ multinomial(theta);
   ...

Simple, but introduces a lot of parameters.

2.  Marginalize the theta out as in the beta-binomial.  The easiest
way to do this would be to define the dirichlet-multinomial as
a function:

functions {
  real dirichlet_multinomial(int[] y, vector alpha) {
     return value based on y and alpha
  }
}

and then use

  y ~ dirichlet_multinomial(alpha);

in the model block.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
In the stochastic volatility model in Section 6.5 of the manual (version 2.8.0), the prior for the volatility of the log volatility {{sigma}} is given as a Cauchy distribution. But this parameter should be strictly positive and in fact there is a constraint to ensure that it is positive. What happens to invalid samples? Is there rejection sampling going on under the covers? Wouldn't it better to choose e.g a Gamma distribution with shape = 0.5 and rate = 0.005 to avoid this?

Dominic.

messages.subject: Re: Priors for Stochastic Volatility
messages.subject_clean: Priors for Stochastic Volatility
messages.body_plain:
On Sunday, November 8, 2015 at 12:34:00 PM UTC-5, Dominic Steinitz wrote:
> In the stochastic volatility model in Section 6.5 of the manual (version 2.8.0), the prior for the volatility of the log volatility {{sigma}} is given as a Cauchy distribution. But this parameter should be strictly positive and in fact there is a constraint to ensure that it is positive. What happens to invalid samples? Is there rejection sampling going on under the covers?

There are almost surely no invalid samples to reject due to Stan's hidden transformations. The declaration in the parameters block that

real<lower=0> sigma;

implies that sigma is actually exp(log_sigma) but you don't declare / define / see log_sigma and Stan handle Jacobian term for you for anything declared in the parameters block (only).

The prior

sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);

places a CONSTANT amount of density on the negative part of the real line where sigma cannot be. So, conceptually this should be a truncated prior

sigma ~ cauchy(0,5) T[0,];

However, the truncation would only subtract the CONSTANT log(1 - 0.5) from the log-posterior, and constants do not affect which proposals get accepted or rejected by the Metropolis test. So, including the truncation would only slow things down and not affect any of the posterior draws. In effect, this amounts to a half-Cauchy prior over the positive numbers.

But, it is far too easy to utilize this shortcut when it is not appropriate; namely, in situations where the median and / or scale of the Cauchy distribution are unknowns in which case the amount of truncated density is not a constant. In those situations, you should either truncate explicitly or use a distribution that is defined for a non-negative variable.

> Wouldn't it better to choose e.g a Gamma distribution with shape = 0.5 and rate = 0.005 to avoid this?

We have mostly stopped advocating Cauchy priors but don't like Gamma priors with such a small rate (or shape) either. It isn't technically necessary to use a prior that is defined only for positive numbers but whether you get efficient sampling for a particular choice of prior also depends a lot on the data.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

I'm assuming that by "Separately, getting convergence in the individual studies is fine, but overall it is proving very problematic.", you mean that once you add hyperpriors for psi, mu and kappa, thinks fall apart. It would be useful if you could point out which parameters do not converge. Also, did you check for divergent iterations (see elsewhere on this list on how to do that in R)?

My first intuition is that study-level parameters mu and psi are going to be highly, positively correlated. The higher mortality rate mu, the fewer mosquitoes are predicted to be around, and thus, the higher the capture rate psi has to be. Any deviations from the exponential survival will be absorbed by the NB sampling error, mediated by kappa.

How much information do you have in your data? Your hyperpriors for mu, psi, and kappa are superweak, and may allow your model to wander. E.g., normal(0,10) for the meanof mu is far too wide; 99% of log-odds are between -5 and 5. You may want to try narrowing your hyperpriors, and see how the model behaves. If it's still aweful, there might be some problems with sampling efficiency related to the posterior geometry (I defer to others to comment on this).

Best,

Luc

messages.subject_clean: applying Bayesian analysis to Extreme Value Theory (EVT)
messages.body_plain:
Excellent, Aki.

One thing I think you need to consider though: Theory says that the tails of most distribution converge to a Generalized Pareto distribution as one moves along their tails toward infinity. Of course our data do not extend to infinity, so we have to stop moving to the right before we run out of data. This then raises the question of whether the GP well approximates the chunk of the tail we examine. So one issue in GP fitting is the choice of the threshold defining the tail. Too high and you have too little data; too low and you are too far from the theoretical GP distribution.

One popular diagnostic in choosing the threshold is the mean residual life plot, which is the average exceedance of all points above a threshold, as a function of possible thresholds. (E.g., see https://books.google.com/books?id=SonbBwAAQBAJ&lpg=PR4&dq=stuart%20coles%20extreme%20value%20theory&pg=PA80#v=onepage&q&f=false.) If a distribution is GP, the MRL will be linear, as shown in the Coles book linked to. So in practice, we look at the MRL plot and ask when it starts to become linear as we move to the right. As you can imagine, one hopes one's conclusions are robust to reasonable changes in the threshold selected; and there is a literature (maybe some of it Bayesian) on more formal methods for choosing the threshold. In effect, it is a third parameter you need to take on board in some way.

Attached is the MRL I used, made with my "extreme" module for Stata. It includes 95% confidence intervals. From this, I chose a threshold of 150, as noted in a footnote in the blog post. Below 150, it seems like there is a statistically significant bend.

So at a minimum it would be interesting to know what happens if you use that threshold, i.e., only fit to the data above 150. Certainly that choice is debatable, and I did not systematically explore alternatives. It appears that you used 100, right?

This matters because, as seems clear, at lower Dst levels the distribution is more power-law like, which if extrapolated produces a fatter tail. So the more of the distribution you fit to, the higher the risk of extremes you will project. To some extent the uncertainty here may be irreducible, since we don't know when GP behavior sets in. But I think some attention to the threshold issue would probably be worthwhile.

--David

Too high and you have too little data; too low and you are too far from the theoretical GP distribution.
>
> One popular diagnostic in choosing the threshold is the mean residual life plot, which is the average exceedance of all points above a threshold, as a function of possible thresholds. (E.g., see https://books.google.com/books?id=SonbBwAAQBAJ&lpg=PR4&dq=stuart%20coles%20extreme%20value%20theory&pg=PA80#v=onepage&q&f=false.) If a distribution is GP, the MRL will be linear, as shown in the Coles book linked to. So in practice, we look at the MRL plot and ask when it starts to become linear as we move to the right. As you can imagine, one hopes one's conclusions are robust to reasonable changes in the threshold selected; and there is a literature (maybe some of it Bayesian) on more formal methods for choosing the threshold. In effect, it is a third parameter you need to take on board in some way.
>
> Attached is the MRL I used, made with my "extreme" module for Stata. It includes 95% confidence intervals. From this, I chose a threshold of 150, as noted in a footnote in the blog post. Below 150, it seems like there is a statistically significant bend.
>
> So at a minimum it would be interesting to know what happens if you use that threshold, i.e., only fit to the data above 150. Certainly that choice is debatable, and I did not systematically explore alternatives. It appears that you used 100, right?
>
> This matters because, as seems clear, at lower Dst levels the distribution is more power-law like, which if extrapolated produces a fatter tail. So the more of the distribution you fit to, the higher the risk of extremes you will project. To some extent the uncertainty here may be irreducible, since we don't know when GP behavior sets in. But I think some attention to the threshold issue would probably be worthwhile.
>
> --David
>

> > As I'm interested in generalized Pareto for other applications, I made a Stan model for the extreme geomagnetic storms discussed at

> >
> > David Roodman kindly provided the n=373 observations shown in the previous (non-Bayesian) analysis.
> >
> > I've attached the Stan code, Matlab code and a figure showing the results. I hope my Matlab code is clear enough to be translated to other environments.

> > Stan doesn't have yet builtin generalized Pareto, so I wrote the necessary log density and ccdf functions, too.
