> > I used uniform priors, since the model has only two parameters and n=373 (data are informative), and I don't have any expert knowledge about geomagnetic storms..

depending on the floating point implementation.

any S, I, or R states then there will be nothing to constrain your parameters
and it wouldn’t be surprising if that non identified posterior stretched into
pathological parameters.

with your initial conditions (say with init=0 or some small value) and
start with a small step size to avoid poor adaptation.

messages.body_plain:
Yes, one of the awkward features of deep hierarchical models (with many layers,
we usually reserve levels to speak about different effects on the same layer)
is that variance grows exponentially fast so you have to have tighter priors than
you might initially consider.  For example, try sampling from the hierarchical prior
and see how much variance you get.  This is also a nice way to tune the priors
to ensure reasonable variance of the top-level parameters.

As Krzysztof notes you’ll also want to be careful about the implementation.
There are 2^{nodes} possible parameterizations but a fully non-centered
one will probably be a good starting point.  You’ll ultimately get something
that looks like

top_level_effect = mean_effect + \prod_{n = 1}^{N_layers} standard_deviation_{n}

The problem here is that you want to infer the discrete parameter N, but Stan can’t fit discrete parameters.
Your best bet is to assume a super population — i.e. a large static population, each with a probability of
being active (in which case they add a pareto distribution to the likelihood) or inactive (in which case they
add nothing to the likelihood).  For an ecological example of this approach see, for example,
https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/master/knitr/dorazio-royle-occupancy/dorazio-et-al-knitr.Rmd

> X ~ Landau  // pdf has the form : 1/pi * integral from 0 to infinity (e ^-(-t*log(t)-xt) * sin(pi * t)) dt)
> M = y_min * lambda (X + ln(lambda))
>
> But then again, can Landau distribution be implemented in stan when it involves integral?

Not unless you can find some analytic form that approximates it well enough.

As far as I know, the only interface to giving a custom distribution to stan is via increment_log_prob, but I was curious if "the passing the lookup table"  is possible.

A lookup table won’t work because it doesn’t provide the associated gradient which is needed for HMC.

messages.subject_clean: applying Bayesian analysis to Extreme Value Theory (EVT)
messages.body_plain:
Aki and Colin,

This exchange has been very stimulating for me. It prompted me this afternoon to develop more fully the reason I hesitated to incorporate the information. But that also led me to want to revise my published estimate upward a bit.

My concern is this. I have an estimator for a parameter. The estimator is imprecise and so has some distribution. My (historically) preferred way of estimating the distribution can put non-zero probability on the belief that the Carrington event was impossible, contradicting reality. Colin seems to propose that I chop off the point mass off the low end of my distribution, which is at 0. Then, evidently, I take the mean or median of the remaining distribution. But I worry that I will systematically bias my central estimate upward by first chopping off one end of the distribution. I will be incorporating a highly nonrepresentative selection of pre-1957 information. Thus while the point mass may look impossible in itself, it may still be better to leave it there in order to keep my central estimate properly centered.

It would be different if we had complete Dst data back to 1859. Or really, it should go back even earlier, since if we keep the data set as short as possible while still embracing that historic extreme, the selection would still be biased. At any rate, if we had all that data, then we could incorporate not only the peak of 1859, but also all the information about the lows that occurred in 1859-57. Right now we are doing the first but not the second.

My theory that imposing Pr[|Dst|>850]>0 induces bias generates a testable prediction wIthin the estimation framework I have used and understand well. If I draw smaller and smaller samples from the data set we are working with, fit the GP to them, and throw out those that predict Pr[|Dst|>850]=0, the median Pr[|Dst|>850] for those that remain should rise. This is because as the samples shrink the estimator's variance grows, producing more extreme probability on the high and low sides. Those on the low side will all be at 0. So as this "tail" grows, chopping it off should induce more bias. On the other hand, if I don't throw away the implausible Pr[|Dst|>850]=0 estimates, the median shouldn't become more biased as the samples shrink.

I tested this with simulations. I found it to be true--after introducing one tweak. Maximum likelihood is biased in small samples; more precisely it has O(n^-1) bias. So shrinking the samples per se tends to change results. To compensate, I applied the Cox-Snell correction for the ML Generalized Pareto estimator. (See eqs 53 & 54 here <http://web.uvic.ca/~dgiles/blog/Giles_Feng_Godwin_revision_2014.pdf>.) Early on I had thought about using this in my published analysis as well. The paper just linked to shows through Monte Carlo simulations that the correction does work. But the paper does not check whether it reduces bias in estimates of return levels and return probabilities, nor whether it improves inference about them. And some preliminary Monte Carlo simulations of my own were discouraging. So I thought I should be careful about grabbing the shiny new thing.

Attached is a graph of the results. Recall that the full event data set has 134 observations (episodes of |Dst|>=100). For each sample size N from 134 down to 134/4 I drew 10,000 datasets of size N, with replacement. For each, I fit the GP, made the Cox-Snell bias correction, and computed the predicted probability Pr[|Dst|>=850 | |Dst|>=100]. I computed the mean and median probability with and without filtering for Pr[|Dst|>=850 | |Dst|>=100]>0.

The results suggest to me that only the unfiltered median is unbiased, or at least that it is less-biased. If I understand right, this would correspond in Aki's work to removing the requirement that Pr[Carrington]>0.

The good experience with the Cox-Snell bias-correction made me more inclined to include it my posted analysis. Here is a graph that incorporates it. If you compare it carefully to the one at http://blog.givewell.org/2015/07/13/geomagnetic-storms-using-extreme-value-theory-to-gauge-the-risk/, you'll see the GP line is slightly higher now. The 95% CI per decade for -850 is now [0%, 5.8%] instead of [0%,4.0%] and the median is 0.56%/decade.

Dinner calls...

--David

David,

Do you see an advantage to your analysis based on finding the ML fit over the Bayesian analysis as Aki has done?   To me the latter seems much more natural.

I suspect you're right that in the context of the analysis you've done, rejecting resamplings for which the ML fit satisfies P(Quebec)=0 or even just the weaker condition that P(Carrrington)=0 doesn't make sense.

In the context of a Bayesian analysis of the data set that includes Quebec of course you automatically have P(Quebec)>0.  Also, it's natural to impose on the prior that P(Carrington)>0.

Colin.

Hi Colin,

                No, I don’t see any strong advantage of the frequentist ML fit over the Bayesian approach, though my understanding of the latter is incomplete. My prior, as it were, is that the two should give similar answers if given similar inputs. Possibly Aki’s next answer will prove me wrong on that.

                (In the bootstrapping method I use, it is of course possible for P(Quebec)=0 in some replications.)

--David

messages.subject: Change point models w/ covariates determined by change point
messages.subject_clean: Change point models w/ covariates determined by change point
messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone, apologies if the answer to this is obvious but I'm struggling to determine the consequences of using a change point in a model that determines not only when parameter estimates should differ, but also how the data itself is summarized into covariates.

For example, let's say I have 2 predictors in a logistic regression model, predictor A and predictor Z.  I have values for these predictors in such a way that across a dataset consisting of 5,000 observations for 50 patients (it's a medical dataset with about 100 measurements per patient) predictor A is always the same for a given patient (as is the outcome) while predictor Z can fluctuate.  I suspect there is a point at which the effect of Z on the outcome dramatically changes, so I'm trying to determine where that split is and what the effects are above and below it.  For example the data may look like:

Patient ID   A       Z      Outcome
1                 1.1    10     1
1                 1.1    5       1
1                 1.1    8       1
...
50                -.8     3      0
50                -.8     21    0
50                -.8     17    0
# 5,000 records total

Now, in a more standard change point model I could say there is a single change point somewhere for Z and that the coefficient for Z above and below that value differs (I've seen plenty of examples out there like that), but that's not what I'm curious about.

What I'm really after though is an answer to this question:

> Is it possible to have the change point in Z determine an aggregation over the values of Z for a given patient and then use those aggregations as covariates, instead of individual values?

For example, if the change point (which I'll call CP), for Z was say 5 I could then summarize the 5,000 record dataset into 50 observations and create two new variables like "Percentage of observations where Z was below CP=5" and "Percentage of observations where Z was above CP=5".  The new data used to generate the log probability in each step might then look like this:

Patient ID   A       pct_of_z_obs_below_CP   pct_of_z_obs_above_CP    Outcome
1                 1.1    .23                                      .77                                        1
2                 0.5    .56                                      .44                                        0
3                 1.9    .81                                      .19                                        0
...
50               -.8     .1                                        .9                                          1
# 50 records total

These values would then be passed into the likelihood function, after multiplying them by their coefficients.

Sure there are other ways to do the modeling that don't involve aggregations of covariates at each step, but for the sake of the mental exercise, is this approach ever valid?  I see that there are already some difficulties in sampling change points with Stan since they induce a discontinuity in the likelihood, but I have no clue what the consequences are of also manipulating the covariate values at each step.  Does anybody have experience with this?

I attached a model that would attempt to do this, if seeing it in code instead is of any help.

Thanks!

messages.subject_clean: Initializing a vector of length one
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a vector which I would like to initialize. In some settings
this vector has length 1 (the context is a GLM where I might only have
an intercept), which breaks the initialization (I think because R
doesn't distinguish between a scalar and a length one vector).
Consider the super simple model:

data {
  int<lower=0> P;
}
parameters {
  vector[P] beta;
}
model {
  beta ~ normal(0,1);
}

Then both sampling and optimizing are fine if P=2:

sm=stan_model("length_one_vector.stan")
P=2
optimizing(sm, dat=list(P=P), init=list(beta=rep(1,P))) # this is fine
sampling(sm, dat=list(P=P), init=list( list(beta=rep(1,P) ) ),
chains=1) # this is fine

But if P=1 then it fails.

P=1
optimizing(sm, dat=list(P=P), init=list(beta=rep(1,P)))
sampling(sm, dat=list(P=P), init=list( list(beta=rep(1,P) ) ), chains=1)
# Error: Initialization from source failed.
# mismatch in number dimensions declared and found in context;
processing stage=initialization; variable name=beta; dims
declared=(1); dims found=()

Trying to initialization beta as a 1x1 matrix doesn't help:

optimizing(sm, dat=list(P=P), init=list(beta=matrix(1,dat$P,1)))
# Error: Initialization from source failed. mismatch in number
dimensions declared and found in context; processing
stage=initialization; variable name=beta; dims declared=(1); dims
found=(1,1)

Obviously I can work around this by having a special case model for
the P=1 case, but that seems in poor taste. Any thoughts much
appreciated.

Thanks a lot

David.

--
David A. Knowles,
Stanford University.
E-mail: know...@gmail.com
Web: http://cs.stanford.edu/~davidknowles/

messages.body_plain:
Only to run multiple chains.

We strongly recommend against those fat inverse gamma priors
for both computational and statistical reasons.  See the manual
chapter on regression for recommendations and our new Wiki:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations

You're probably better off with a direct Cholesky-factor
parameterization, but if you want to create your own 2 x 2 matrix,
then instead of this

>
> T[1,2] <- r * sigma[1] * sigma[2];
> T[2,1] <- r * sigma[1] * sigma[2];

you want to reuse the element:

T[2,1] <- T[1, 2];

And you want to vectorize this the other way
around:

> for (i in 1:n)
> x[i] ~ student_t(nu, y[i], sigmaerror);
> }"

x:  (n x 2)
y:  (n x 2)
nu: (2 x 1)
sigmaerror: (2 x 1)

by insteading reordering

x: (2 x n)
y: (2 x n)

so you can do this:

  for (k in 1:2)
    x[k] ~ student_t(nu[k], y[k], sigmaerror[k]);

That vectorizes all the elements together with the same mean
and sd, which allows the relevant subexpressions to be reused.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
That's a good example to use to give people
a taste of what we've been talking over for the
future syntax of Stan, which will involve

1.  vectorizing all of our functions,

2.  allowing compound declare and define statements, and

3.  adding a syntax for piping single terms or collections of
    terms to the log density accumulator.

Then that program below would look like this:

  vector[K] a <- conc * softmax(beta * x[n]);
  real suma <- sum(a);
  ld<< lgamma(suma),
       lgamma(a + y[n]),
       -lgamma(suma + sum(y[n])),
       -lgamma(a);

Stay tuned.

- Bob

Thank you, Aki.

I did not intend to imply that I thought we ought to require Carrington/850 to be possible. I just asked about that to try to understand better what you did. I do think however that this is pretty much what Colin was looking for.

In my bootstrapping, the only constraint is sigma>0. Except in the “filtered” regressions in the graph in my last message, I require 850 to be possible.

I tend to think now that just introducing this requirement introduces a kind of bias. Maybe there is a name for this in Bayesian analysis, right? If I am interested in inference about a parameter k and I introduce the prior k > kmin based on the historical record, but choose not to impose a max based on the historical record, then this in itself tends to raise my central estimate of k, right? Is there a name for this phenomenon?

--David

messages.body_plain:
Stan assumes that the model plus transforms define
a continuously differentiable density.  For now, we only
use first-order gradient information.

If there are kinks at the boundaries of the piecewise
function, Stan could have trouble sampling across boundaries
unless step sizes are small enough that the discontinuity in
derivatives doesn't affect the slice rejection step in NUTS.

- Bob

Hi Charles,

Welcome to the list.

On Thu, Nov 12, 2015 at 3:24 PM, charlesm93 <charles.ma...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hello, and thank you ahead of time for your help.
>
> I am writing a C++ function, which I hope to contribute to stan/math.

Great.

I've read through your email and I don't think you'll want to take that approach, but I could be mistaken. There needs to be some clarification: I'm still not sure what you're trying to do.

>
> The function returns a random variable Y, and takes a combination of data and parameters as its input. If I understand correctly, Y and the parameters are auto-diff variables, with type stan::math::var.

I'll need some clarification with what you're calling a "random variable."

Is the function a random number generator where on multiple calls it's returning different values?
  or
Is the function returning a class of some sort that knows about its distribution and sufficient stats?
  or
Is the function a deterministic function of its inputs?

We don't have a "random variable" type in the Stan Math Library and my guess is that you're actually describing the third option.

> My function computes the value of Y, but it does not compute its adjoint.

This is where I'm beginning to think it's the third option: a deterministic function of the inputs.

If you're only getting as far as computing the function value, my guess is that the function could be written in the Stan language and it'll be as fast as writing the function in C++ directly. Could you tell us what the function does?

>
> Will stan/math automatically compute the adjoint of Y if I stick to operators defined for autodiff variables?

Yes.

> Do you recommend I template my function so that it deals both with variables of type double and stan::math::var?

In order for the function to be useful in the Stan math library, it will need to template all arguments to the function this way.

It's the beauty of how the Stan language generates fully templated functions that allow any combination of autodiff variables (stan::math::var) and scalar constants (double; we don't get the gradients with respect to these arguments).

> I am making these assumptions based on this conversation: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/contributing$20function$20C$2B$2B/stan-users/YxiFyUirPU4/ku23AQzJzjMJ

Sorry -- that's a really long thread and it feels out-of-date. Feel free to ask more questions!

>
> Clarification and suggestions are more than welcomed!

I think what would help immensely is if you provided either a Stan function, some pseudocode, or even the C++ implementation that you have now.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
> On Nov 12, 2015, at 3:24 PM, charlesm93 <charles.ma...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello, and thank you ahead of time for your help.

Thanks for moving the discussion over the mailing list.

> I am writing a C++ function, which I hope to contribute to stan/math.
>
> The function returns a random variable Y, and takes a combination of data and parameters as its input. If I understand correctly, Y and the parameters are auto-diff variables, with type stan::math::var.
>
> My function computes the value of Y, but it does not compute its adjoint.
>
> Will stan/math automatically compute the adjoint of Y if I stick to operators defined for autodiff variables?

Yes.  But you don't get any added efficiency over defining
the function directly in Stan. What happens is the function
definition itself gets autodiffed at run time, which can take
up lots of memory and/or time compared to having analytic gradients.

For efficiency in reverse mode (what we use for gradients
in all of our algorithms) you can define your own vari instance
and use that instead.  You can see how to do that in the autodiff
paper or in the code that gets compiled for user-defined functions
through the language.

Just make sure to promote the intermediate values you need.

> Do you recommend I template my function so that it deals both with variables of type double and stan::math::var?

Yes, see the section of the arXiv paper about promotion using
Boost.  All the intermediate values have to be promoted to
the highest type, where math::var > double.

> I am making these assumptions based on this conversation: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/contributing$20function$20C$2B$2B/stan-users/YxiFyUirPU4/ku23AQzJzjMJ
>
> Clarification and suggestions are more than welcomed!

There's also a wiki page on how to add new user-defined functions
so that they are visible through the language.  The key point is
adding to the symbol table.  In that case, they absolutely need to
be definable so that any continuous variables can be instantiated
as either double or var or fvar (the reverse-mode autodiff).

- Bob

Bob,

In order to prevent work-arounds my suggestion is to rewrite
neg_binomial_2_rng(mu,psi) as suggested by Ben:
real gamma_temp;
if (is_inf(psi))
  gamma_temp <- mu;
else
  gamma_temp <- gamma_rng(psi, psi / mu);
if (gamma_temp < pow(2.0, 30.0))
  result <- poisson_rng(gamma_temp);
else
  result <- normal_rng(gamma_temp, sqrt(gamma_temp));

Thank you,
Linas

You've got to stop thinking about bias as the end all be all.  Aki's model takes the lower bound into account by assuming compatibility with the assumed generalized Pareto distribution, which is uses the data in a self-consistent way.  Imposing an explicit lower bound lilies by the data need not be self consistent and hence can lose information in the posterior.

The only worry in Aki's model is not that there is bias, because again it is self consistent and hence optimal conditioned on the modeling assumptions, but rather that the modeling assumptions themselves may be wrong.  Now looking at the predictive check it's not hard to see an elbow that the generalized Pareto is too rigid to fit, but again this an issue with the assumed tail and not the lower bound.

On Friday, November 13, 2015 at 11:44:54 AM UTC-5, Chris Weber wrote:
> I have a really basic question, which I just can't seem to figure it out. I have a two category variable with a lot of missing data. It's my understanding that the easiest way to deal with this -- since Stan doesn't sample discrete parameters -- is to marginalize over the missing data.

Assuming a binary outcome is Missing At Random, then it is relatively easy to deal with the missingness using the log_mix() function

increment_log_prob(log_mix(p, bernoulli_logit_log(1, p), bernoulli_logit_log(0, p)));

where p is the probability of success, which may be a function of some other parameters. What this is doing is getting the log probability if y were 1 and weighting that by p and then adding the log probability if y were 0, weighted 1 - p.

However, in an IRT context, the Missing at Random assumption is usually implausible (even if you are ostensibly conditioning on latent ability) because students skip questions that they initially have trouble answering or fail to make it to the end of the test in time because they struggled too much with the questions at the beginning of the test. In that case, you should also somehow be modeling a binary variable that indicates whether the student answered the question.

Ben

messages.subject: Splitting Hierarchical Data to Improve Vectorization
messages.subject_clean: Splitting Hierarchical Data to Improve Vectorization
messages.body_plain:
My sense is that when using groups Stan likely spends a lot of time in loops when there are opportunities to use vectorization.

In the attached code, I created an unbalanced panel of about 190,000 observations. I allow the mean to vary between five groups. In the original Stan regression, I use a loop and effectively a lookup to get the correct mean to use. In the alternate method, I split the data up before I put it into Stan, so that I can take advantage of vectorization better.

In one run, the original method takes 320.8s on my work machine (4 chains, average: 80.2s), while the alternate method takes 67.4s (4 chains, average 16.9s). So it gave a nearly 5x speed up. As this is just one simple test, I'm not sure how much this is influenced by the number of groups or their size.

To me, the biggest downside to this approach is that it is much less flexible. It requires splitting up data and hard-coding the different groups in the Stan file. This suggests that maybe there is scope for improvements to the Stan language to facilitate this type of data (and so that Stan can recognize it and adjust things properly to take into account the vectorization).

For instance, in my approach, I am doing the regression with centered data because I didn't feel like putting in individual-level intercepts for the purpose of demonstrating this. The individual-level intercept version runs significantly slower (I believe it is more accurate, but I'm a little worried by it since the intercept is correlated with the group means). However, if Stan could, on its end, split up the data into the relevant groups and then just apply the correct normal vector sum to each, then I think it could be much faster.

I don't recall seeing this as a recommended strategy anywhere to speed up Stan code. I can put in a Github issue if this is original.

The files are merely to demonstrate the difference in performance. Not an actual application. But yes, the idea is to fit an intercept-only model with different intercepts for the groups but with the same standard deviation. The ff.stan file should produce similar results as the ff_alt.stan file, but with a different implementation. ff.stan fits a different mean to each of the groups with the same error, while ff_alt.stan splits the data up into separate inputs before putting the data in stan.

The N_obs variable is in ff.stan, but in ff_alt.stan there is a separate one for each of the inputs because it is an unbalanced panel and not all of them are the same length. I guess what's not used in ff_alt.stan is N, not N_obs. That's just some extra stuff that got carried over (for instance the ff.stan file also has a tt variable that is superfluous, the result of changes I had made to simplify it and didn't entirely clean up, sorry).

With respect to your point about collapsing the expression graph, I was just speculating as to my point about loops.

With respect to aggregating data, I see a sub-section on exploiting sufficient statistics. I had seen that example, but assumed that it was really just another approach to vectorization. I don't really know what exploiting sufficient statistics means and it isn't explained in the manual beyond saying "hey this is a thing". I googled it and the wikipedia page on sufficient statistics has a section on the normal distribution. Maybe my approach is similar to that...but I would have never thought that this idea was in the manual. Anyway, I don't consider this approach like aggregating data. Maybe more like de-aggregating data (or manually de-grouping hierarchical data).

messages.body_plain:
I believe in the example you sent you could go a step
further by using the sufficient stats for the normal to
compute the posterior analytically.  A sufficient stat is
just a summary stat of data that is enough information for
estimtion.  It only works in exponential families.

But even the aggregation you're doing will help, as you
saw.  Basically anything that gets the data into a
vectorized form to reduce the expression graph size and
reduce redundant calculations will help.

I'll add a note to that effect in the manual.  I'm not sure
what you meant by adding a GitHub issue --- were you thinking
we could somehow automate this, or was it just about the doc?  If
it's just about the doc, I added the note here for the next manual:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1617#issuecomment-156593302

Thanks.

- Bob

P.S.  We have an arXiv paper that goes into the gory details of
the autodiff if you're interested --- that's where all the
purely computational efficiency considerations are (there are
also statistical considerations like fatness of tails and
varying posterior curvature which can motivate reparameterizations).

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] abs(x) is evil, but what about sqrt(square(x))?
messages.body_plain:
:-)  Insofar as Stan does the right thing with functions
and derivatives, sqrt(square(x)) is just a less efficient
way to implement abs(x).

Not being differentiable at 0 can be a problem in that
neighborhood with the Hamiltonian simulation, but the
bigger issue is the multimodality typically introduced
by the symmetry around 0 making p(x, ...) = p(-x, ...).
It's a classic case of non-identifiability.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
If you have a parameter with a beta(1, 1e7) prior, you should be rescaling it.  Recall the principle that all parameters should be scale-free (an important principle which is not actually in my book, unfortunately).

> On Nov 13, 2015, at 9:28 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> If you want two values alpha and beta such that 0 < alpha + beta < 1,
> then you can do this:
>
>  real<lower=0, upper=1> alpha;
>  real<lower=0, upper=(1 - alpha)> beta;
>
> It's a stick-breaking process where alpha breaks off a piece
> from (0,1) and then beta breaks off a piece of what's left.
> It's the same construction our simplex constraint uses.
> Stan takes care of the Jacobians for constrained variables,
> so you can use the resulting variables without adjusting for
> changes of variables.
>
> - Bob
>
> P.S.  This kind of thing could cause numerical issues:
>
>>  PCT_Initial ~ beta(1,1000000);
>
> It's going to put most of the prior mass very close to 0.
> At least it's better than putting it close to 1 numerically.
>
>

skewed one you get for logit(Y) from Y ~ beta(1, 1d6).

distribution when you marginalize the nuisance parameters

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am working on an IRT model with several indicators. From what I've read I know there can be benefits to pulling the parameters for each indicator from a multivariate normal distribution for example (A_k, B_k) ∼ Multivariate Normal ( mu_k, Sigma_k), for each k indicator (where A_k an B_k are the difficulty and discrimination parameters). At the same time though to identify the IRT I want to constrain B_k > 0.  I cannot figure out though how to go about this in Stan. There seems to be two options.

1) When I declare the the parameters to constrain B_k > 0. But, I think (and tell me if I am wrong) that since I am pulling them from a multivariate normal I have to declare A_k and B_k as a single vector (Parameters_K). Since this is a single vector I cannot find a way to only constrain part of the vector (just the second value).

2) To use truncation when sampling: multi_normal(mu_k, Sigma_k) T[0,]; But again, it seems that this will apply to both parameters.

As of now I've been just using the absolute value of the B_k, but that seems like a poor way to accomplish this goal.

Is there something simple I have been missing?

Thanks so much for any help,

Kevin Reuning

From what I've read I know there can be benefits to pulling the parameters for each indicator from a multivariate normal distribution for example (A_k, B_k) ∼ Multivariate Normal ( mu_k, Sigma_k), for each k indicator (where A_k an B_k are the difficulty and discrimination parameters). At the same time though to identify the IRT I want to constrain B_k > 0.  I cannot figure out though how to go about this in Stan. There seems to be two options.
>
> 1) When I declare the the parameters to constrain B_k > 0. But, I think (and tell me if I am wrong) that since I am pulling them from a multivariate normal I have to declare A_k and B_k as a single vector (Parameters_K). Since this is a single vector I cannot find a way to only constrain part of the vector (just the second value).

You can declare them separately

parameters {
  real A[K];
  real<lower=0> B[K];
}

At this point, you could compose a bivariate normal with truncation as a marginal normal distribution for A[k] times a conditional normal distribution for B[k] given A[k] that is truncated at 0.

> 2) To use truncation when sampling: multi_normal(mu_k, Sigma_k) T[0,]; But again, it seems that this will apply to both parameters.

Actually, I don't think truncation works for any multivariate density.

> As of now I've been just using the absolute value of the B_k, but that seems like a poor way to accomplish this goal.

Yes. Counter productive even because of the bimodality and the confusion it causes to the Hamiltonian when B[k] cross zero.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On Sunday, November 15, 2015 at 5:54:40 PM UTC-5, Chris Weber wrote:
>
> Sorry -- it should read:
>
>  increment_log_prob(log_mix(gamma, bernoulli_log(m, gamma), bernoulli_logit_log(y[n], alpha[kk[n]]*theta[jj[n]]- beta[kk[n]])
>
> Since bernoulli_log collects the log probability that a value is missing (m is the vector of missing data), gamma should represent theta -- the probability that a value is missing. Why can't this value then be used in the first argument, which is also probability that a value is missing? I understand this is overly simplistic, and I could also model the probability that a value is missing, but shouldn't it work?

It is even simpler.
For each unit that is observed, you have bernoulli_log(y[i,j], p) where p = Pr(y = 1 | x)
For each unit that is missing, you need a mixture of the two possibilities (y = 1 and y = 0) where the mixing weight is again p = Pr(y = 1 | x). So, that would be log_mix(p, bernoulli_log(1, p), bernoulli_log(0, p)).
For each observation,  you need another likelihood contribution for q = Pr(m = 1 | z), which is just bernoulli_log(m[i,j], q).

I can't see any reason why you would want to impose the constraint that p = q.

Ben

Hi Bob,

We're certainly aware of the work going on at both US and EU Novartis sites and have been in contact with Wenping and Sebastian. Our main reason for working on the development of such code is because the Novartis code is not publicly available and we do not know if and when it will be. In addition it's a useful exercise for us to learn Stan architecture.

Why program in C++ versus Stan? While Stan is a pretty rich programming language, C++ is more so. In particular it permits object-oriented approaches and a richer collection of data types that make it easier to deal with some of the complications of event schedules encountered in pharmacometric analyses. (Sorry for preaching to the converted.)

In particular it permits object-oriented approaches and a richer collection of data types that make it easier to deal with some of the complications of event schedules encountered in pharmacometric analyses. (Sorry for preaching to the converted.)

That's reasonable, but it's really hard to make sense of the request when we don't know what computation is actually taking place.

Unfortunately, we haven't documented all of the internals of Stan, but there are some key requirements like the ability to instantiate the templated function under all combinations of double and stan::math::var that need to be met.

The effort of implementing functions in C++ level starts to pay off once you have analytic or at least computable gradients for each of the arguments of the function. Until then, I don't usually think it's worth the effort. With that said, if some functions are being used multiple times, the right place to focus would be to add a way to include functions using some sort of directive. We've looked into that, but it's just on our backburner.

With this particular function, it would really help to have some pseudo-code or a Stan function so we can try to understand the intention and provide better advice.

messages.body_plain:
For Stan, cite the paper for the algorithms and the
software for the software.

Theano and Stan are both very much latecomers to their
respective games.  There have been tools around since
as early the 1980s if not earlier doing autodiff and
symbolic diff.

For autodiff, there's a standard textbook (Griewank and Walther),
a newer book (Naumann), and a full chapter in Nocedal and Wright's
classic Numerical Optimization book.

Theano isn't autodiff by the way --- it's symbolic diff.
See the discussion of the pros and cons in our autodiff
paper.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Per,

I'm not sure what you mean by "offsets in parameter estimations", but I don't think you should be worried. rstan::extract with inc_warmup=TRUE will return the draws for iteration 1 through the final iteration. You can prepend the initial values obtained from get_inits() manually if you want to, but either way the only draws you should use for inference are those that comprise the post-warmup posterior sample (the combined post-warmup draws from all chains).

Hope that helps, but let me know if I've misunderstood your question.

Jonah

messages.body_plain:
Looks like nobody responded here.  I've been trying to lay
off these complicated-looking modeling issue posts hoping
better statisticians would respond.

You can build the simple change-point model where each patient
has a change at some point or where there is a shared change.

I didn't understand your aggregation scheme, but if you can
write the likelihood down, you can probably code it in Stan.

And if it's really just a mental exercise, we're awfully busy
for that kind of thing!  I think that's one reason I put this one
on the backburner.

- Bob

> On Nov 12, 2015, at 8:24 AM, Eric Czech <eric.all...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hey everyone, apologies if the answer to this is obvious but I'm struggling to determine the consequences of using a change point in a model that determines not only when parameter estimates should differ, but also how the data itself is summarized into covariates.
>
> For example, let's say I have 2 predictors in a logistic regression model, predictor A and predictor Z.  I have values for these predictors in such a way that across a dataset consisting of 5,000 observations for 50 patients (it's a medical dataset with about 100 measurements per patient) predictor A is always the same for a given patient (as is the outcome) while predictor Z can fluctuate.  I suspect there is a point at which the effect of Z on the outcome dramatically changes, so I'm trying to determine where that split is and what the effects are above and below it.  For example the data may look like:
>
> Patient ID   A       Z      Outcome
> 1                 1.1    10     1
> 1                 1.1    5       1
> 1                 1.1    8       1
> ...
> 50                -.8     3      0
> 50                -.8     21    0
> 50                -.8     17    0
> # 5,000 records total
>
> Now, in a more standard change point model I could say there is a single change point somewhere for Z and that the coefficient for Z above and below that value differs (I've seen plenty of examples out there like that), but that's not what I'm curious about.
>
> What I'm really after though is an answer to this question:
>
> Is it possible to have the change point in Z determine an aggregation over the values of Z for a given patient and then use those aggregations as covariates, instead of individual values?
>
> For example, if the change point (which I'll call CP), for Z was say 5 I could then summarize the 5,000 record dataset into 50 observations and create two new variables like "Percentage of observations where Z was below CP=5" and "Percentage of observations where Z was above CP=5".  The new data used to generate the log probability in each step might then look like this:
>
> Patient ID   A       pct_of_z_obs_below_CP   pct_of_z_obs_above_CP    Outcome
> 1                 1.1    .23                                      .77                                        1
> 2                 0.5    .56                                      .44                                        0
> 3                 1.9    .81                                      .19                                        0
> ...
> 50               -.8     .1                                        .9                                          1
> # 50 records total
>
> These values would then be passed into the likelihood function, after multiplying them by their coefficients.
>
>
> Sure there are other ways to do the modeling that don't involve aggregations of covariates at each step, but for the sake of the mental exercise, is this approach ever valid?  I see that there are already some difficulties in sampling change points with Stan since they induce a discontinuity in the likelihood, but I have no clue what the consequences are of also manipulating the covariate values at each step.  Does anybody have experience with this?
>
> I attached a model that would attempt to do this, if seeing it in code instead is of any help.
>
> Thanks!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jonah,

thank you for your reply.

What I meant with "offsets in parameter estimations", was if one expects rstan::extract to return the entire chain, including all warmup and post-warmup samples, with the very first sample having the value that you specified as the initial value, then if the very first sample does NOT have the specified initial value, it could imply that all samples had been shifted with this value: difference = specified initial value - actual initial value.

For my final inference I only use post-warmup samples :)

However, I almost always inspect the entire traceplot of both warmup and post-warmup samples, to see if I can improve my sampling efficiency by tweaking my priors, warmup lengths, initializations etc.

Best,
Per

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Conditional Logistic Regression in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
Stata's clogit and asclogit seem to correspond to sections 17.4.4 (A Conditional Fixed Effects Estimator) and 18.2.3 (The Conditional Logit Model), respectively, of Greene's Econometric Analysis 7ed and both fall under the Logit Model in chapter 3 of Train's Discrete Choice 2ed, which includes all logit models in which IIA holds (meaning homoscedastic and uncorrelated errors, if remember the conditions correctly). Greene explains the different names while Train lumps these models together, which I find more useful because the difference comes from your data and what interactions you are trying to infer, rather than from the mathematics.

As Ben guessed, I am interested in nested / mixed logit models as these terms are used in economics. These models relax the IIA assumption but it will probably be more appropriate to discuss them in another thread . I thought Kruschke's terminology is the Bayesian way to refer to nested logit but that doesn't seem to be the case. messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to fit the "blocker" Stan model from the WinBUGS example models.  Running this as given (although removing the delta_new line), using the default sampler parameters works (although I get a handful of iterations which hit max_treedepth; increasing this to 15 fixes this).

The Stan model file uses a t distribution:

  delta  ~ student_t(4, d, sigma_delta);

Whereas the original WinBUGS model uses a normal. Setting the Stan model to use a normal distribution:

 delta  ~ normal(d, sigma_delta);

gives me divergent transitions; typically about 50 after warmup (over the default 2000 total iterations over 4 chains).   I can eliminate these by increasing adept_delta to 0.99 (at the expense of the model running much more slowly)

I've read a few threads on stan-users about divergent transitions, but I'm not sure why I'm seeing them here; it looks like a fairly simple "standard" example.  I'd previously encountered divergent transitions on a more complex network meta-analysis model I was trying to write, except here I wasn't able to eliminate them by increasing adapt_delta (in the end I switched back to JAGS for this, which I'm more familiar with).

It'd be good to get an understanding of what's going on; can anyone offer any advice?  I realise I can fix the problem for this example by adjusting the sampler settings, but it'd be good to know what it is about the problem that's making it difficult for Stan to solve.  How worried should I be about still (occasionally) hitting max_treedepth? (I've tried setting this even higher, but still get the odd iteration that reaches it).

I've attached the model files I'm running and an R script to run them.

Thanks

David

PS I am getting the occasional warning:
[1] "The following numerical problems occured the indicated number of times on chain 3"
                                                                                   count
Exception thrown at line 23: student_t_log: Scale parameter is 0, but must be > 0!     1
[1] "If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,"
[2] "but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified."

But as this is only occurring sporadically I'm assuming I shouldn't worry too much about it?

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

I'm definitely not the best person to answer this, though I guess I am the one available first ;)

It looks to me like mu and delta should be constrained both in the variable definition, and the distribution (using, say, lognormal), to be positive. If not, you have a negative standard deviation, which is an obvious no-no, and therefore a model misspecfication. (i.e. "your model may be... or misspecified")

The reason it's happening only occasionally is because those values move away from 0 - since the correct value is obviously higher. Not fixing it shouldn't break anything, but that explains what's going on, if that is clear to you.

Cheers,
David

I get errors specifying iter=0 or chains=0. In the end I just pulled some code out of optimizing. In case its of use to others:

get_sampler=function(object, data) {
  rstan:::prep_call_sampler(object)
  model_cppname <- object@model_cpp$model_cppname
  mod <- get("module", envir = object@dso@.CXXDSOMISC, inherits = FALSE)
  stan_fit_cpp_module <- eval(call("$", mod, paste('stan_fit4', model_cppname, sep = '')))
  stopifnot(is.list(data))
  parsed_data <- rstan:::parse_data(get_cppcode(object))
  for (i in seq_along(data)) parsed_data[[names(data)[i]]] <- data[[i]]
  parsed_data <- parsed_data[!sapply(parsed_data, is.null)]
  new(stan_fit_cpp_module, parsed_data, object@dso@.CXXDSOMISC$cxxfun)
}

Then I can just do

sampler <- get_sampler( my_stan_model, data )
sampler$grad_log_prob( theta, T )

Thanks for your help anyway.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical heteroscedastic measurement error--- unstable?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Hierarchical heteroscedastic measurement error--- unstable?
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure if this is your problem, but you have a potentially
very fat-tailed prior on x and only a single observation x_meas to fit
each parameter x with.

You can also have problems with parameters like B0 that you expect
to be around 53.  Stan has to figure that out during adaptation.  We
often recommend the non-centered style parameterization of this, where you'd
have

  B0_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
  B0 <- B0_raw + 53;

And similarly for beta, with

  beta_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
  beta <- beta_raw * maxSlope;

- Bob

P.S. I find this kind of thing:

  B0 + beta *( x -2.)

very hard to read compared to the more standard

  B0 + beta * (x - 2)

or even "2.0" in place of "2" (you only need to do that if
all the expressions are integers and you don't want the
rounded down integer result).

pseudo-healthy data best.

Is this remotely reasonable? Are there standard methods / formulations
for this sort of problem amenable to Stan's inference algorithms?

(sorry for the rather generic question)

Marmaduke

>
> Maybe a better question, or at least one more specific to the mechanics of Stan, is:
>
> If the likelihood is not continuously differentiable with respect to a certain parameter, is it absolutely necessary to manually marginalize over it (in the transformed parameters block)?

It depends.  If it's just a small kink in an otherwise differentiable
function, that's one thing, but if it's a discontinuity in the underlying
function, then small step size won't cope.

> Or put another way, what are the consequences of just letting Stan randomly sample something like a change point?  In some small simulated datasets I created both approaches seem to work but I'm just not sure what to expect from Stan in that case with larger, more realistic datasets.

Stan can't do discrete sampling.  You can use a continuous
changepoint, then do conditionals, but there's no way to get
information back to the changepoint sampling that way, so it'll
reduce to an accept/rejection algorithm, which is bad news.

- Bob

Sounds like you know more about this model now than we do.
A t-distribution will have fatter tails than a normal, so
won't be so harsh in constraining parameter values to a narrow
range.

We do not recommend uniform(0, 10) priors, but if you insist
on using them, you have to make the constraints match, as in:

  real<lower=0, upper=10> sigma;

At which point, you don't need the uniform(0, 10) thing as
the default is uniform on values satisfying constraints.

The problem with values getting close to 0 is that they're
log transformed, so they can underflow pretty easily if that's
where there's support in the model.

- Bob

increment_log_prob(log_mix(p[i], bernoulli_logit_log(1,p[i]), bernoulli_logit_log(0, p[i])));

when m==1 (m is coded 0 when y is observed 1 when y is missing). p is the conditional probability of y=1.

It seems to be a common issue, and it just wasn't clear to me how to implement this in stan. Thanks

On Saturday, November 21, 2015 at 9:38:01 AM UTC-5, Chris Weber wrote:
> I have an IRT model. As is often the case, I have a fair amount of missing data. In the past, I've used JAGS with these models, and as you know, NAs are permitted. So, I'm trying to figure out something comparable here that doesn't require dropping the data.
>
> The sample code I've included, is just a variant of the IRT model in the manual. Rather than dropping the data, I'm trying to account for the missing data. The problem is that y is a discrete variable. One of the suggestions seems to be to use a mixture approach to do this. Ben had suggested that for y_miss, I use:
>
> increment_log_prob(log_mix(p[i], bernoulli_logit_log(1,p[i]), bernoulli_logit_log(0, p[i])));
>
> when m==1 (m is coded 0 when y is observed 1 when y is missing). p is the conditional probability of y=1.
>
> I'd rather do something other than drop the data.If this is the wrong approach, then I'm honestly not sure what the correct approach should be.

I think what Bob and I are saying is that if you believe, prior to seeing the data, that a binary random variable Y is distributed Bernoulli with some probability p (that may vary from observation to observation as a function of the IRT stuff), how could you possibly believe that the likelihood contribution for a missing outcome is anything other than

log_mix(p, bernoulli_log(1, p), bernoulli_log(0, p))

which is equivalent to but less stable than

log_mix(p, bernoulli_logit_log(1, eta), bernoulli_logit_log(0, eta))

where p = inv_logit(eta)? To believe anything else about a missing outcome would be contradictory. Just make eta a vector and modify the previous expression to

increment_log_prob(log_mix(inv_logit(eta[i]), bernoulli_logit_log(1, eta[i]), bernoulli_logit_log(0, eta[i])));

whenever m[i] == 1. If m[i] == 0, then you just have

increment_log_prob(bernoulli_logit(y[i], eta[i]));

> At this point, I'm fine with assuming MAR. This is a large cross sectional survey, in which questions were randomized, so that seems reasonable to me.

With nothing else, the above would assume MAR conditional on the student's latent ability, but even for a dataset like PISA where some students are asked some questions but not others by the design of the research, you still have some missingness on questions a student was actually asked, which provides additional information on the student's (lack of) ability. The most obvious reasons why a student would not answer an asked question are that it seemed difficult and / or it was toward the end of the test and the student never got to it. Thus, it is pretty easy to construct another likelihood contribution for m, which could also be a logit model and does not require any mixing because m is observed for all students and all questions.

In the case where a student is not asked a question by design, that is not a random variable and does not contribute anything to the likelihood.

Ben

On Saturday, November 21, 2015 at 12:33:02 PM UTC-5, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> With nothing else, the above would assume MAR conditional on the student's latent ability, but even for a dataset like PISA where some students are asked some questions but not others by the design of the research, you still have some missingness on questions a student was actually asked, which provides additional information on the student's (lack of) ability. The most obvious reasons why a student would not answer an asked question are that it seemed difficult and / or it was toward the end of the test and the student never got to it. Thus, it is pretty easy to construct another likelihood contribution for m, which could also be a logit model and does not require any mixing because m is observed for all students and all questions.
>
> In the case where a student is not asked a question by design, that is not a random variable and does not contribute anything to the likelihood.

Another way of saying the same thing is that the observed data of a student on a test question are one of
Observed to be the correct answer
Observed to be the incorrect answer
Unobserved but the student would have given the correct answer to that question
Unobserved but the student would have given the incorrect answer to that question

So, you need a likelihood function for that four-headed monster. The usual way of proceeding (the "selection" approach) is to factor this as

Pr(y, m | stuff) = Pr(y | stuff) * Pr(m | y, stuff)

In the situations where a student was not asked a particular question by design, them Pr(m | y, stuff) = Pr(m | stuff). In other words, whether the student would have gotten that question correct tells you nothing about the probability that the student would have an opportunity to answer the question (which was determined by the research design alone). That is the MAR case and you don't have to mess with Pr(m | stuff).

Conversely, whether the student would have gotten the answer right or wrong tells you a lot about the probability would answer a question that was, in fact, asked. In other words, Pr(m | y, stuff) != Pr(m | stuff) and you need a model for Pr(m | y, stuff). That could be anything but at least seems to depend on the difficulty of the question and the position of the question in the test.

All this is a bit more tedious in Stan than BUGS because HMC needs derivatives and thus cannot do discrete unknowns. So, when m = 1 (and thus y is missing), we have to write

Pr(y, m = 1 | stuff) =  Pr(y = 1 | stuff) * Pr(y = 1 | stuff) * Pr(m = 1 | y = 1, stuff) +
                        Pr(y = 0 | stuff) * Pr(y = 0 | stuff) * Pr(m = 1 | y = 0, stuff)

Also HMC utilizes the logarithm of the posterior density, so if you take the logarithm of both sides, on the right hand side, you get a log of a sum of exponentials,

log(Pr(y, m = 1 | stuff)) = log(exp(log(Pr(y = 1 | stuff)) + log(Pr(y = 1 | stuff)) + log(Pr(m = 1 | y = 1, stuff))) +
                                exp(log(Pr(y = 0 | stuff)) + log(Pr(y = 0 | stuff)) + log(Pr(m = 1 | y = 0, stuff))))

which is what the log_mix() function facilitates by wrapping log_sum_exp() (which is why you may see both forms in the User Manual). And since Pr(y = 0 | stuff) = 1 - Pr(y = 1 | stuff), you only have to pass Pr(y = 1 | stuff) to the first argument of log_mix(). The second and third arguments to log_mix() are the two things being mixed together on the log scale, which are at first log(Pr(y = 1| stuff)) and log(Pr(y = 0 | stuff)). You could call log_mix() again to mix log(Pr(m = 1 | y = 1, stuff)) and log(Pr(m = 1 | y = 0, stuff)) in the NMAR case.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: applying Bayesian analysis to Extreme Value Theory (EVT)
messages.subject_clean: applying Bayesian analysis to Extreme Value Theory (EVT)
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Aki, David, Michael, this has been a really interesting discussion.

A key issue for policy is the probability of a really extreme storm, like the Carrington event.  Under the ML distribution, David found a probability of ~0.005% per solar storm, which works out to 0.33% per decade or 6.4% probability of at least one over a 200 year period.  As David noted in his original post, those numbers seem low.  Indeed, eyeballing Aki's charts, we see numbers about a factor of 20x larger on a Bayesian analysis:  a probability of >0.1% per storm which works out to ~6% per decade or a probability of ~80% (computed as 1-(1-6%)^20 = 81%) over a 200 year period.

That's a sufficiently large difference that I would describe it as qualitative:  Under the ML distribution, one could describe Carrington as a freakishly extreme event, that humanity was unlucky to have encountered in the period since the Industrial Revolution and thus should have limited weight in policy planning.  Under a Bayesian analysis that incorporates contributions from the non-ML distributions, we instead see Carrington as a magnitude of storm that might plausibly recur in the coming decades and so is very important for planning.

Hi Colin,

I think that summary is correct, but I would add that the simulations I did showed that if the last ~200 years are statistically identical to the observed 1957-2014 Dst history aside from Carrington, then estimates that factor in the Carrington occurrence and nothing else from pre-1957 will be upward-biased. So somehow I think we need to build in some prior about the pre-1957 Dst history.

Something that might help is the aa index (https://www.ngdc.noaa.gov/stp/geomag/aastar.html), which I believe is based on two antipodal, non-equatorial observatories and goes back to 1868. Maybe it can be used to estimate pre-1957 Dst values.

Aki, I’m not sure if this speaks to what you were thinking about exploring time dependency, but two cycles I would include are the semi-annual cycle, with peak Dst activity at the equinoxes, and the sunspot cycle, which I treat as taking 11 years and reaching a low on 1 Jan 2008.

--David

messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin,

You're right about the behavior, and it might indeed be bizarre, but it's not specific to rstan. It's how R and ggplot2 behave in general. For example:

library(ggplot2)

x <- rnorm(100)
qplot(x) # this will display a plot

for (j in 1:10) {
 x <- rnorm(100)
 qplot(x) # no plot displayed
 print(qplot(x)) # plot displayed
}

But this isn't only with ggplot2. For example:

2 + 2 # the number 4 is printed

for (j in 1:10) {
 2 + 2 # nothing is printed
 print(2 + 2) # 4 is printed
}

For the rstan plotting functions that return a single ggplot object this is how they will behave. I suppose we could have them always call print internally, but then this would deviate from the typical behavior you get when using ggplot2.

Jonah

On Sunday, November 22, 2015 at 10:40:43 AM UTC-5, David Roodman wrote:
>
>
>
> I think that summary is correct, but I would add that the simulations I did showed that if the last ~200 years are statistically identical to the observed 1957-2014 Dst history aside from Carrington, then estimates that factor in the Carrington occurrence and nothing else from pre-1957 will be upward-biased. So somehow I think we need to build in some prior about the pre-1957 Dst history.
>

It's of course good to include more history if you can. But to be clear, I don't think there's a bias in the Bayesian analysis from including Carrington in the minimal way Aki did.  As I understand it, he only required that the process be consistent with the possibility of a Carrington-scale event.

Fundamentally, what's going on here I think is the ML distribution may not give you a reasonable approximation of the probability of a really extreme event.  I think most of the probability density for a Carrington-scale event comes from lower likelihood distributions with much greater density there.  (I'm not trying to make a mathematically precise statement.  But if I were to try, the flavor would be something like:  Define a "really extreme event" as a function of sample size n as an event that occurs O(1) times. Then you might see even in the limit n->infinity that the ratio of the probability from the ML distribution over the true probability might converge to something less than 1. Aki, I downloaded the aa index data from ftp://ftp.ngdc.noaa.gov/STP/GEOMAGNETIC_DATA/AASTAR/aaindex. A version that may be easier to work with is at http://1drv.ms/1T8Xfqi.

From: stan-...@googlegroups.com [mailto:stan-...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of Colin Rust

Sent: Sunday, November 22, 2015 5:56 PM
To: Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com>

Subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: applying Bayesian analysis to Extreme Value Theory (EVT)

On Sunday, November 22, 2015 at 10:40:43 AM UTC-5, David Roodman wrote:
>
>
>
> I think that summary is correct, but I would add that the simulations I did showed that if the last ~200 years are statistically identical to the observed 1957-2014 Dst history aside from Carrington, then estimates that factor in the Carrington occurrence and nothing else from pre-1957 will be upward-biased. So somehow I think we need to build in some prior about the pre-1957 Dst history.
>
>

It's of course good to include more history if you can. But to be clear, I don't think there's a bias in the Bayesian analysis from including Carrington in the minimal way Aki did.  As I understand it, he only required that the process be consistent with the possibility of a Carrington-scale event.

Fundamentally, what's going on here I think is the ML distribution may not give you a reasonable approximation of the probability of a really extreme event.  I think most of the probability density for a Carrington-scale event comes from lower likelihood distributions with much greater density there.  (I'm not trying to make a mathematically precise statement.  But if I were to try, the flavor would be something like:  Define a "really extreme event" as a function of sample size n as an event that occurs O(1) times.  So the definition of really extreme varies with the sample size.  Then you might see even in the limit n->infinity that the ratio of the probability from the ML distribution over the true probability might converge to something less than 1.  On the other hand, if you had a fixed definition of "extreme" rather than one that depended on n, then it would converge to 1.)

--

messages.body_plain:
Hi
I'm a bit lost of what to do when WAIC and LOO give the opposite results with real data. I'll explain further

I'm using Rstan and I'm comparing two models, one is a shifted lognormal distribution, basically:

...
lognormal_log(y- psi,mu,sigma)

and the other one is a mixture between that distribution and a uniform distribution which should be a contaminated distribution:

...

P_dist[1] ~  beta(0.1,0.9);

  for (i in 1:N_obs){
    real distrib[2];
    distrib[1] <-  log(P_dist[1])+ uniform_log(rt[i],range_rt[1],range_rt[2]);
    distrib[2] <-  log(P_dist[2])+ shifted_lognormal_log(rt[i],mu[i], sigma,psi[i]);
    increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(distrib));
  }
with shifted_lognormal_log is just a function that does what I showed before.

Both work relatively well after I increased the tree depth (just that the intercept of the distributions has an Rhat of 1.02, but since it recovers the parameters I didn't have the patience to run the code for longer time). I tried the models with simulated data and they recover the parameters quite well. If I generate data with the contaminated distribution, and I use the package loo, and the function compare, both waic and loo agree that the second model has a weight of 1.

Now when I try to compare the two models in a realistic dataset I get this:

> compare(loo_sl,loo_sl_mixt)
elpd_diff        se   weight1   weight2
     -6.6       8.2       1.0       0.0
> compare(waic_sl,waic_sl_mixt)
elpd_diff        se   weight1   weight2
      2.5       7.0       0.1       0.9

>From Vehtari et al 2015, I understand that "for influential observations WAIC underestimates the effect of leaving out one observation". And that LOO "relies on inference from a smaller subset of the data being close to inference from the full dataset". So my objective is to figure out if this uniform distribution is good enough to capture the outliers, or if I must try something else. How can I check which of the compare results is telling me what I want to know?

Thanks!
(By the way, I was pretty sure that there was a tag for modeling comparison, but it's no longer there (or maybe it was never there), I hope my question is still relevant to the mailing list)

Bruno

I think I got the algebra wrong last time.  Here's the
right thing:

  log_mix(p, bernoull_log(1, p), bernoulli_log(0, p))

  = log_mix(p, log(p), log(1 - p))

  = log(p * exp(log(p)) + (1 - p) * exp(log(1-p)))

  = log(p * p + (1 - p) * (1 - p))

  = log(p^2 + 1 - 2p + p^2)

  = log(2 * p^2 - 2p + 1)

So it doesn't reduce to a no-op.  So this is missing
missingness information or something?  I still don't understand
why p is used twice here.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I'm creating an R package for internal use that depends on rstan, and I'm struggling with how to handle that dependency. It's considered a bad idea to call library() from within package code -- instead you include it in the Imports line in the DESCRIPTION file. But stan() and sampling() seem to require a prior explicit call to library(rstan) in order to work. If you just call rstan::stan() without previously issuing the command "library(rstan)", you get the following error:

    Error in .Object$initialize(...) :
      could not find function "cpp_object_initializer"
    failed to create the sampler; sampling not done

I have tried creating a .onLoad() function in my package, with a call to loadNamespace("rstan"), but I still get the same error.

Another issue with creating a package is that you want to precompile the model files. I've never been able to figure out where the DLL actually gets stored or how to transfer it to another machine with the same architecture and OS.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Missing Categorical Data
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, November 23, 2015 at 1:10:30 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>   = log(2 * p^2 - 2p + 1)
>
> So it doesn't reduce to a no-op.  So this is missing
> missingness information or something?  I still don't understand
> why p is used twice here.

The fact that an observation is missing is almost always known. Maybe try thinking of it like this: If we were using BUGS and y[i] were NA, at each iteration BUGS would draw a realization of the binary outcome from its full-conditional distribution, which is just Bernoulli(p). Now imagine drawing a lot of realizations of that binary outcome from a Bernoulli(p) and taking the log of the average Bernoulli PMF over the realizations. In R code that would be,

p <- 2 / 3 # or whatever depending on the student and the IRT stuff
y <- rbinom(n = 10^6, size = 1, prob = p)
log(mean(dbinom(y, size = 1, prob = p))) # about 0.588
log(1 - 2 * p + 2 * p^2) # basically also 0.588

In Stan, we can't draw from a Bernoulli in a model block, but we can evaluate log(1 - 2 * p + 2 * p^2) or equivalently log_mix(p, bernoulli_log(1, p), bernoulli_log(0, p)) to get a likelihood contribution for Pr(y | stuff) when y is missing. Then we need another likelihood contribution for the same observation(s) that is Pr(m = 1 | y, stuff), which would be another Bernoulli mixture that now marginalizes over the missing predictor (y) unless we made the assumption that Pr(m = 1 | y, stuff) = Pr(m = 1 | stuff).

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, November 23, 2015 at 11:20:50 AM UTC-5, Chris Weber wrote:
> In terms of the four-headed monster (great term....I completely agree), if we factor p(y,m) in the usual selection specification....so,
>
> Pr(y, m | stuff) = Pr(y | stuff) * Pr(m | y, stuff)
>
> Are you sure the likelihood contribution, when m==1 is:
>
> Pr(y, m = 1 | stuff) =  Pr(y = 1 | stuff) * Pr(y = 1 | stuff) * Pr(m = 1 | y = 1, stuff) +
>                         Pr(y = 0 | stuff) * Pr(y = 0 | stuff) * Pr(m = 1 | y = 0, stuff)
>
> it's not clear whey there are two pr(y=1|stuff) and pr(y=0|stuff) terms....

There are two such terms because one comes from the factorization

Pr(y, m | stuff) = Pr(y | stuff) * Pr(m | y, stuff)

and the other comes from the fact that we have to mix the above over the two possibilities for the unknown y. In other words, the mixing weight on the y = 1 branch is Pr(y = 1 | stuff) and the mixing weight on the y = 0 branch is Pr(y = 0 | stuff) = (1 - Pr(y = 1 | stuff)). So, we get

Pr(y, m = 1 | stuff) =  Pr(y = 1 | stuff) * y1_branch + (1 - Pr(y = 1 | stuff)) * y0_branch
                     =  Pr(y = 1 | stuff) * [Pr(y = 1 | stuff) * Pr(m = 1 | y = 1, stuff)] +
                        Pr(y = 0 | stuff) * [Pr(y = 0 | stuff) * Pr(m = 1 | y = 0, stuff)]

Ben

messages.subject: rstan 2.8.1 released
messages.subject_clean: rstan 2.8.1 released
messages.body_plain:
A new version of rstan was released on CRAN last week and by now binaries are available for Windows and any Mac OS since Mavericks. I, however, forgot to commit the NEWS file, so there is no indication as to what changed. Since StanHeaders was not updated, there are no changes in what Stan can do, only changes in the R code surrounding it. There were some bugs that were fixed, although a couple more were apparently introduced and already discovered:
Passing arguments through the ... of stan() will not work directly because they get passed to stanc() accidentally. This includes chain_id, init_r, test_grad, refresh, and enable_random_init. To work around this, you can first call stan_model() and then pass that to sampling() along with init_r, refresh, etc. Or you can install rstan from github
devtools::install_github("stan-dev/rstan", ref = "v2.8.1-1", subdir = "rstan/rstan")
Calling expose_stan_functions() on a .stan file with print() statements in user-defined Stan functions will not work at the moment. You can comment out the print() statements or shortly call
source("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stan-dev/rstan/develop/rstan/rstan/R/expose_stan_functions.R") # R >= 3.2.2 or
devtools::source_url("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stan-dev/rstan/develop/rstan/rstan/R/expose_stan_functions.R")

The main goal of rstan 2.8.1 was to get ready for the release of the rstanarm package, which has been basically usable for a couple months but is not on CRAN yet because a few things are still missing. If you have rstan >= 2.8.1 installed already, you can install rstanarm for testing via
devtools::install_github("stan-dev/rstanarm", local = FALSE)
For those of you that do not already know, rstanarm is a package that has several Stan programs that are compiled at (or before) installation time, a few R functions that call these Stan programs using the conventional "formula, data, other_arguments" R syntax, and a bunch of R functions that analyze and / or plot the results.

To get rstanarm onto CRAN (in the near future) we had to overcome the problem that Kevin, Sebastian, and others have asked about how to write an R package that comes with Stan models and works on all platforms (including 32 bit Windows). The rstan 2.8.1 package has two functions that make this much easier, whereas it was pretty much impossible with rstan <= 2.8.0.
The stanc_builder() function is a lot like stanc() --- which you may or may not have ever called directly but is what parses a Stan program and outputs the corresponding C++ --- but has two differences.
The obfuscate_model_name argument defaults to FALSE (whereas it defaults to TRUE in stanc). This means that the C++ class defining the model has a predictable name rather than a randomly-generated one (which prevents name clashes in conventional rstan use).
The stanc_builder() function --- unlike stanc() --- reads a .stan file into R, replaces lines that have C++ style #include statements with the included files, and writes the amalgamated .stan file to the tempdir() before parsing and compiling it. For example, you can have something like
functions {
  #include "common_functions.txt"
}
and stanc_builder will find the file called "common_functions.txt" (looking in the same directory as the .stan file by default but there is an isystem argument that can be specified as a different directory to look in) and put it where #include "common_functions.txt" appears to yield something like
functions {
  vector sqrt_vector(vector x) {
    vector[rows(x)] out;
    for (i in 1:rows(x)) out[i] <- sqrt(x[i]);
    return out;
  }
}
if common_functions.txt consisted solely of that sqrt_vector function. These C++-style include statements can be used anywhere in a Stan program but are not chainable (i.e. common_functions.txt cannot #include "helpers.txt"; you have to #include "helpers.txt" in your Stan program first and then #include "common_functions.txt" second). Basically, this makes it possible to maintain an informal library of Stan functions and code snippets that can be reused in multiple Stan programs without having to copy-and-paste a bunch of duplicated code. The rstanarm package uses this mechanism extensively. Right now, we have 1170 lines of code spread over six .stan files and 388 lines of code spread over 13 .txt files that are #included into many of those six .stan files.
The rstan.package.skeleton() function works a lot like base R's package.skeleton() function and Rcpp's rcpp.package.skeleton() function in that it will create a directory that has an outline of what is needed to create a R package of Stan programs that are driven by rstan (which is put under Imports in the DESCRIPTION file). The rstan.package.skeleton() function downloads some GPLv3 code from the rstanarm GitHub repository to make this work, so either be comfortable with licensing your R package under the GPLv3, or don't distribute your R package outside your company, or don't use these downloaded files. Basically a package like rstanarm has the following minimal structure:
-rwxr-xr-x 1 goodrich goodrich  287 Oct 18 14:49 cleanup       # downloaded from rstanarm
-rwxr-xr-x 1 goodrich goodrich  287 Oct 18 14:49 cleanup.win   # downloaded from rstanarm
-rw-r--r-- 1 goodrich goodrich 1433 Nov 18 00:06 DESCRIPTION   # created by rstan.package.skeleton
drwxr-xr-x 2 goodrich goodrich 4096 Oct 31 16:26 exec          # a subdirectory for Stan programs and #included .txt files
drwxr-xr-x 2 goodrich goodrich 4096 Nov 23 01:35 man           # you need to fill this in, as usual for an R package
-rw-r--r-- 1 goodrich goodrich 3241 Nov 23 01:35 NAMESPACE     # you need to fill this in, as usual for an R package
drwxr-xr-x 2 goodrich goodrich 4096 Nov 20 17:16 R             # some code downloaded from rstanarm; fill in the rest
-rw-r--r-- 1 goodrich goodrich  211 Nov  1 13:54 .Rbuildignore # downloaded from rstanarm
drwxr-xr-x 3 goodrich goodrich 4096 Nov 23 00:53 src           # a few files are autogenerated by rstan.package.skeleton
drwxr-xr-x 2 goodrich goodrich 4096 Oct 31 11:28 tools         # downloaded from rstanarm
The cleanup and cleanup.win bash files are called when you do R CMD build or R CMD INSTALL --preclean but in this case, they ironically create C++ files in the src/ directory by executing an R helper file in tools/, which looks for files with a .stan extension under exec/, parses them with stanc_builder(), and glues all the C++ together under src/ (otherwise you will get linker errors that we have not figured out yet). At that point, R CMD INSTALL including R CMD INSTALL --build will work "as usual" for an R package that has Rcpp-style C++ files, which is to say both the 64bit and 32bit shared objects will be built under libs/ unless --no-multiarch is passed. This is the only mechanism that is currently known to work for packages with pre-built Stan programs and many other mechanisms are known to not work in some respect. So, if you want to create a package like rstanarm that comes with pre-built Stan programs, this is the best way to go. Inside the package's namespace, there will be a named list of objects of stanmodel class (with corresponding entries under the RcppModules line in DESCRIPTION) that are essentially equivalent to what you could get if you called stan_model("foo.stan"). In particular, your package's R functions can pass them to rstan::sampling() or rstan::optimizing(). You may also want to put rstanarm in Imports or Suggests and utilize the generic functions we have written for analyzing the results. Or consider making a pull request on GitHub to have your code incorporated into rstanarm. But if you decide to maintain an R package yourself, it is best to follow rstanarm's wake. Otherwise, it will be more difficult for us to upload new versions of rstan without breaking the R packages that depend on it.

Ben

This many khats>1 means trouble and means that you can't trust IS-LOO nor WAIC, and you need to use k-fold-CV or change your model to be more robust. I know you had log-uniform part for the contamination, but I don't think that uniform with some interval is necessarily a good choice as you get discontinuity in the density. How about making the second component to be a wider log-normal distribution?

The fact that you don't have khats>1 with the simulated data shows that your real data is more surprising. You could check the observed values with khat>1

More complex model may have larger khats as then these influential observations can change the posterior more (making importance sampling leave one out approximation more difficult). The log-uniform is likely to be problematic, too..

Diagonal line in the plots would help, but you can see that most of points behave nicely and you can see how the mixture model change the values, but then you can also the group of problematic points.

Aki
