> > > >
> > > > > On Nov 24, 2015, at 12:47 PM, Ryan Batt <bat...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > Hi all,
> > > > >
> > > > > I decided to try Stan because I was starting to find computation time in JAGS to be limiting for the models I was running, and I had plans to increase model complexity even more. I've put together my first Stan model, and I'm a little nervous because the run time is quite long even for a small fraction of the full data set. I've read quite a bit of the manual, and found some wonderfully helpful examples on this mailing list, too.
> > > > >
> > > > > My model is a minimal example that I think retains some of the essential elements of its complexity. I've tried making some changes to improve performance, but I'm still running rather slowly (taking about 15 minutes for ~1/1E4 of the full data set, and before introducing additional complexities/ parameters). So I was hoping I could get some pointers on where to focus my efforts before I begin hacking away.
> > > > >
> > > > > The model
> > > > >
> > > > > The model is similar to what can be found here: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/occupancy/stan-users/Jc0Wej7XCKI/qalSXkVdUacJ
> > > > >
> > > > > It's also an extension of this paper by Zipkin et al., which extends the previous example in a few ways, most notable of which is by adding covariates.
> > > > >
> > > > > The presence/ absence data come in a 4-dimensional array, X, with the following dimensions:
> > > > >         • year (time, t)
> > > > >         • site (a 1º grid, j)
> > > > >         • sample (a repeated visit to a site, k)
> > > > >         • species (s, or n ... sorry in advance for any confusion)
> > > > > There are two main components to the model:
> > > > >         • Ψ (Psi) is the probability of a species being present
> > > > >         • Θ (Theta) is the probability of detecting a species, given that it's present
> > > > > Each of these probabilities is a linear function of covariates and associated coefficients (parameters). The coefficients vary among species, in a manner such that all species-specific parameters are drawn from the same parent distributions.
> > > > >
> > > > > The observations come from X, but the true presence/ absences are in Z, a latent parameter matrix of 1's and 0's (I used Bob Carpenter's code as an example of how to marginalize this out). There's also a weird parameter, w, which is a binary (1, 0) indicating whether a given species is "real" (available to be sampled).
> > > > >
> > > > > The model looks something like this:
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > ​
> > > > > U and V have dimensions K x nV and K x nU, where K is the maximum number of samples taken from any site in any year, and nV and nU are the number of covariates. The parameters
> > > > > matrices α and β have dimensions of nV x S and nU x S, respectively; the S parameters in each row are drawn from Normal distribution, giving rise to a different parameter for each species. The parameter array  is of length T (number of years), and for each t, it has a length (S) with definition .
> > > > >
> > > > > In words, the model uses covariates to predict both presence/ absence and detectability. The presence/ absence parameters vary hierarchically among species. The covariates are sample-specific (they are things like "day of year" for detection, and "temperature" for presence/absence). In addition, there's a parameter that determines whether or not a species is even real, and this parameter is drawn from a parent distribution whose sole parameter is a year-specific average probability of any given species being part of the supercommunity.
> > > > >
> > > > > The Code
> > > > > I've attached an R script which contains the data, Stan model, and R code to run the model. This data set is a tiny subset of what I'll be working with, but I think it's substantial enough to illustrate some of the challenges with the data.
> > > > >
> > > > > In particular, I had to use a weird workaround to handle sites that weren't sampled in some years, and the fact that each site-year combination has a different number of samples (K). I still presented the data and covariates in an array, but I turned the NA's to 0's. Then, I have a matrix called "nK" that indicates the number of samples in a given site-year. When an element of nK is 0, it means that that site wasn't sampled (I don't think this happens in the example data set). When looping through the data, I don't loop through the full extent of the covariate/ response arrays, instead stopping the loop at the sampled extent.
> > > > >
> > > > > It is worth noting that the sites are not arbitrary, as the same site might be sampled repeatedly in different years. Thus, I may introduce site-specific parameters in the future. On the other hand, the distinction between the k=1 and k=K samples is arbitrary. Thus, it might be possible to recode the samples using the ragged array format (although I can't figure out how to do this with the degree of nesting I have), and it could be possible to recode the sites using a data base format, but not the ragged array format.
> > > > >
> > > > > The Problem
> > > > > My code runs slowly. I'm pretty sure it's because it isn't coded efficiently. I tried using matrix algebra and vectorized operations when I could, but I ran into trouble here because of the raggedness of the samples/ sites (see above). I also wasn't sure how to code the ragged array examples given that my situation is a fair bit more complex than any examples I could find. I was thinking of reparameterizing the distributions to, e.g., use normal(0,1) for alpha and beta, and re-scale them elsewhere. I didn't do this yet because it is my impression that this will help things converge more quickly, but not run more quickly. Right now it seems that regardless of how fast this code converges, it'll still be kinda slow (I'm probably showing my ignorance here).
> > > > >
> > > > > I tried to be careful in how I arranged my dimensions, and my choice of containers. I read through the manual, and tried to optimize the order in which I looped through arrays and matrices.
> > > > >
> > > > > Lastly, I have a hunch that there might be something I did wrong when repurposing some of Bob Carpenter's code. He had written that code for a case where the samples didn't have covariates, so the response variable could be Binomial instead of Bernoulli, and where the parameters (e.g., even Psi and Theta) didn't change among sites, so some of those operations could have been vectorized. Some of the statistical/ coding strategies don't really apply to my data, and while I tried to adapt that code properly, I may have done so in an very inefficient way.
> > > > >
> > > > > Any help with how to improve this model (in the context of these unwieldy data) would be appreciated. The mode may seem complicated, but it's actually going to get a fair bit more complex. It's also working right now, so maybe it was a fair starting point. Thank you for reading through this description, and I apologize for the errors I undoubtedly made in specifying the model here.
> > > > >
> > > > > Attached is the code.
> > > > >
> > > > > Best,
> > > > >
> > > > > Ryan

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Looking for help with the performance of an occupancy model
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've been working to make as many improvements as I could. Thanks to Max and Bob for some insights.

I boiled Bob's original suite of comments down to a to-do list of optimizations to try. I re-wrote the call to `stan()` to only do 50 iterations for each chain, so that the code would run quickly for testing. The attached R file includes all changes I've made since the original posting. At the end of the code I've included the calculation of metrics that I used to measure speed/ efficiency.

Before I made any changes, the code ran in 33.9 sec. These timings are generally from only 1 trial run. Typically stable within a second or so. Does not include compilation time (see attached code).

Please note: A 1 second savings here could end up saving much more time (hours? days?) when the model is run for more chain iterations (e.g., 5k instead of 50) and for the full data set (but making this extrapolation to full data set is tricky). Currently the array containing species abundance is 3x3x7x15 (for these tests). The full data set is 32x99x13x466 + (that last dimension gets padded with, say, 100+ never-seen species) (and I have similar data sets for 11 regions). So even a little savings in these tests will make a big difference in the end.

Here are the list of changes suggested, in the order that I made the changes, and the associated timings:
Don't use if() statements to avoid going into a loop when K=0; `for (k in 1:0) {` will skip the loop anyway.
34.4 sec
(I hadn't started doing seconds/ effective sample size yet)
Move `1 ~ Bernoulli(Omega[t])` out a few levels of for() loops, using `increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(1, Omega[t]) * N * sum(nK[t]))` instead
33.4 sec
(didn't calculate efficiency)
vectorize `alpha[u,s] ~ normal(` and similar for beta; Thought this would require transpose, but it didn't
31.6 sec
0.89 sec per sample (denominator is average nEff across all parameters; see attached)
use tighter priors than cauchy(0, 2.5); I did cauchy(0,2) on the sd, and cauchy(0,1) on the mu; originally tried cauchy(0,1) for both, but that was slower/ less efficient than current
32.8 sec
0.87 sec per sample
Make Psi and Theta local variables that are no longer tracked or reported in end (I can recalculate on my own if needed)
31.6 sec
0.52 sec per sample
Use matrix algebra for calculating each Psi and Theta (no transpose needed). Used `block()` to adapt the size of covariate matrix (U or V) to the number of K in that site-year, so not wasting computations for when `Kmax` is much larger than most `nK[,]` (in some cases there are ~100 K, but only for 1 site-year, e.g.). Avoids many empty elements of Psi and Theta, too.
29.0 sec
0.48 sec per sample
Try vectorizing the calculation of log probabilities. To do this, I decided to aggregate my process covariates (U) over the sample (K) dimension. Then I tried creating vectorized form of the `lp_obs()` function (`lp_obs2()`), and created a new `lp_exists()` function that can works in both of the situations covered by `lp_obs()` and `lp_unobs()`. I struggled with this step, mostly due to matching of types and those cascading effects. I had made some intermediate changes when working towards this that I didn't save, but were a fair bit faster, but didn't include my attempt to vectorize the `lp_obs()` functions. But I forget exactly what I'd had.
22.9 sec
0.72 sec per sample
I have not implemented this yet: Make Omega hierarchical, and/or put it on logit scale (see Bob comments)
As you can see, things have improved. I struggled a lot with #7, and as a result I am hesitant to attempt a similar vectorization for the never-seen species.

As a side note, I found it cumbersome that I could not store integers in a matrix, because Bernoulli requires integer values to be supplied. I found my work arounds, but it was trying. Along those lines, many of the container formats I chose were the result of iterative trial and error; it was hard to get everything to match up correctly for the functions, but I'm learning.

I would greatly appreciate any further comments, but I understand that I may be asking a lot, and I'm very happy with the feedback I've gotten thus far. Thank you all.

-Ryan

> > > > > >
> > > > > > The model
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The model is similar to what can be found here: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/occupancy/stan-users/Jc0Wej7XCKI/qalSXkVdUacJ
> > > > > >
> > > > > > It's also an extension of this paper by Zipkin et al., which extends the previous example in a few ways, most notable of which is by adding covariates.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The presence/ absence data come in a 4-dimensional array, X, with the following dimensions:
> > > > > >         • year (time, t)
> > > > > >         • site (a 1º grid, j)
> > > > > >         • sample (a repeated visit to a site, k)
> > > > > >         • species (s, or n ... sorry in advance for any confusion)
> > > > > > There are two main components to the model:
> > > > > >         • Ψ (Psi) is the probability of a species being present
> > > > > >         • Θ (Theta) is the probability of detecting a species, given that it's present
> > > > > > Each of these probabilities is a linear function of covariates and associated coefficients (parameters). The coefficients vary among species, in a manner such that all species-specific parameters are drawn from the same parent distributions.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The observations come from X, but the true presence/ absences are in Z, a latent parameter matrix of 1's and 0's (I used Bob Carpenter's code as an example of how to marginalize this out). There's also a weird parameter, w, which is a binary (1, 0) indicating whether a given species is "real" (available to be sampled).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The model looks something like this:
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > ​
> > > > > > U and V have dimensions K x nV and K x nU, where K is the maximum number of samples taken from any site in any year, and nV and nU are the number of covariates. The parameters
> > > > > > matrices α and β have dimensions of nV x S and nU x S, respectively; the S parameters in each row are drawn from Normal distribution, giving rise to a different parameter for each species. The parameter array  is of length T (number of years), and for each t, it has a length (S) with definition .
> > > > > >
> > > > > > In words, the model uses covariates to predict both presence/ absence and detectability. The presence/ absence parameters vary hierarchically among species. The covariates are sample-specific (they are things like "day of year" for detection, and "temperature" for presence/absence). In addition, there's a parameter that determines whether or not a species is even real, and this parameter is drawn from a parent distribution whose sole parameter is a year-specific average probability of any given species being part of the supercommunity.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The Code
> > > > > > I've attached an R script which contains the data, Stan model, and R code to run the model. This data set is a tiny subset of what I'll be working with, but I think it's substantial enough to illustrate some of the challenges with the data.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > In particular, I had to use a weird workaround to handle sites that weren't sampled in some years, and the fact that each site-year combination has a different number of samples (K). I still presented the data and covariates in an array, but I turned the NA's to 0's. Then, I have a matrix called "nK" that indicates the number of samples in a given site-year. When an element of nK is 0, it means that that site wasn't sampled (I don't think this happens in the example data set). When looping through the data, I don't loop through the full extent of the covariate/ response arrays, instead stopping the loop at the sampled extent.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > It is worth noting that the sites are not arbitrary, as the same site might be sampled repeatedly in different years. Thus, I may introduce site-specific parameters in the future. On the other hand, the distinction between the k=1 and k=K samples is arbitrary. Thus, it might be possible to recode the samples using the ragged array format (although I can't figure out how to do this with the degree of nesting I have), and it could be possible to recode the sites using a data base format, but not the ragged array format.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The Problem
> > > > > > My code runs slowly. I'm pretty sure it's because it isn't coded efficiently. I tried using matrix algebra and vectorized operations when I could, but I ran into trouble here because of the raggedness of the samples/ sites (see above). I also wasn't sure how to code the ragged array examples given that my situation is a fair bit more complex than any examples I could find. I was thinking of reparameterizing the distributions to, e.g., use normal(0,1) for alpha and beta, and re-scale them elsewhere. I didn't do this yet because it is my impression that this will help things converge more quickly, but not run more quickly. Right now it seems that regardless of how fast this code converges, it'll still be kinda slow (I'm probably showing my ignorance here).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I tried to be careful in how I arranged my dimensions, and my choice of containers. I read through the manual, and tried to optimize the order in which I looped through arrays and matrices.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Lastly, I have a hunch that there might be something I did wrong when repurposing some of Bob Carpenter's code. He had written that code for a case where the samples didn't have covariates, so the response variable could be Binomial instead of Bernoulli, and where the parameters (e.g., even Psi and Theta) didn't change among sites, so some of those operations could have been vectorized. Some of the statistical/ coding strategies don't really apply to my data, and while I tried to adapt that code properly, I may have done so in an very inefficient way.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Any help with how to improve this model (in the context of these unwieldy data) would be appreciated. The mode may seem complicated, but it's actually going to get a fair bit more complex. It's also working right now, so maybe it was a fair starting point. Thank you for reading through this description, and I apologize for the errors I undoubtedly made in specifying the model here.

> > > > > > Best,

messages.body_plain:
There's a chapter in the Stan manual on what all the MCMC
numbers mean.  The mean for each parameter is the estimate
of the posterior mean based on all the MCMC draws --- it's
just the average of all the draws for that parameter.

Multimodality introduces all kinds of headaches.

As for output into CSV format, that is the basic output
from CmdStan (each row is a draw).  In RStan, there's an
extract() function for a fit object.  If you're using another
interface, let us know.

- Bob

to verify everything's working and avoid the possiblity

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, November 26, 2015 at 8:42:27 AM UTC-5, Craig Wang wrote:
> My question is: I'm going to call the same *.stan file 1,000 times for different simulated data, is there a way to only call the C++ translation once to save time?

Yes, in RStan and PyStan. In RStan, it should not compile the same model repeatedly within the same R session, but you can have it not compile repeatedly across R sessions by first calling

rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)

In both RStan and PyStan, you can pass an existing object produced by stan() to the fit argument of stan() to use the same model with different data.

> sample code:
>
> for (i in 1:1000){
>   dat <- data[[i]]
>   m2 <- stan(file="model.stan", data=dat,iter=100000, chains=1,thin=10)
>   var[i]<-1-mean(m2@sim$samples[[1]]$var)
>   }

With Stan, we do not recommend doing 100000 iterations, one chain, or thinning like you might do with a Gibbs sampler or Metropolis-Hastings. The default arguments are more than fine the vast majority of the time. You should read about the differences between how Stan does MCMC relative to a Gibbs sampler or Metropolis-Hastings before doing a bunch of simulations. Also, we do not recommend using syntax like @sim$samples[[1]]$. Use mean(extract(m2, pars = "var", permuted = FALSE)) or something.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Small update on timings.

I decided to let this model chug on a larger-sized data set (32x99x13x466 + 10 0's , so 476). Same model and stan call as in the previously-attached R script. It's been running for ~12 hours now, and the chains are 44%, 52%, 30%, and 28% done (of only 50 iterations; I'm running this on 4 cores, 1 for each chain).

I think that having 31 year-specific dummy variables in V, and 32 non-hierarchical Omega could be hurting things a bit. But this still seems a lot slower than what I would have hoped for. If it takes 24 hours for this model to run, I guess for 5000 iterations it would take a cool .... 100 days? Ouch.

I should also point out that the last dimension there (the 466) is the number of species. Most of them are observed only a handful of times, so this is quite sparse.

I point out these timings just to emphasize my motivation for speeding the code up. Suggestions are welcome.

Oh, and happy Thanksgiving everyone!

Ryan

On Wednesday, November 25, 2015 at 10:56:04 PM UTC-5, Ryan Batt wrote:

> Hi all,
>
> I've been working to make as many improvements as I could. Thanks to Max and Bob for some insights.
>
> I boiled Bob's original suite of comments down to a to-do list of optimizations to try. I re-wrote the call to `stan()` to only do 50 iterations for each chain, so that the code would run quickly for testing. The attached R file includes all changes I've made since the original posting. At the end of the code I've included the calculation of metrics that I used to measure speed/ efficiency.
>
> Before I made any changes, the code ran in 33.9 sec. These timings are generally from only 1 trial run. Typically stable within a second or so. Does not include compilation time (see attached code).
>
> Please note: A 1 second savings here could end up saving much more time (hours? days?) when the model is run for more chain iterations (e.g., 5k instead of 50) and for the full data set (but making this extrapolation to full data set is tricky). Currently the array containing species abundance is 3x3x7x15 (for these tests). The full data set is 32x99x13x466 + (that last dimension gets padded with, say, 100+ never-seen species) (and I have similar data sets for 11 regions). So even a little savings in these tests will make a big difference in the end.
>
> Here are the list of changes suggested, in the order that I made the changes, and the associated timings:
> Don't use if() statements to avoid going into a loop when K=0; `for (k in 1:0) {` will skip the loop anyway.
> 34.4 sec
> (I hadn't started doing seconds/ effective sample size yet)
> Move `1 ~ Bernoulli(Omega[t])` out a few levels of for() loops, using `increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(1, Omega[t]) * N * sum(nK[t]))` instead
> 33.4 sec
> (didn't calculate efficiency)
> vectorize `alpha[u,s] ~ normal(` and similar for beta; Thought this would require transpose, but it didn't
> 31.6 sec
> 0.89 sec per sample (denominator is average nEff across all parameters; see attached)
> use tighter priors than cauchy(0, 2.5); I did cauchy(0,2) on the sd, and cauchy(0,1) on the mu; originally tried cauchy(0,1) for both, but that was slower/ less efficient than current
> 32.8 sec
> 0.87 sec per sample
> Make Psi and Theta local variables that are no longer tracked or reported in end (I can recalculate on my own if needed)
> 31.6 sec
> 0.52 sec per sample
> Use matrix algebra for calculating each Psi and Theta (no transpose needed). Used `block()` to adapt the size of covariate matrix (U or V) to the number of K in that site-year, so not wasting computations for when `Kmax` is much larger than most `nK[,]` (in some cases there are ~100 K, but only for 1 site-year, e.g.). Avoids many empty elements of Psi and Theta, too.
> 29.0 sec
> 0.48 sec per sample
> Try vectorizing the calculation of log probabilities. To do this, I decided to aggregate my process covariates (U) over the sample (K) dimension. Then I tried creating vectorized form of the `lp_obs()` function (`lp_obs2()`), and created a new `lp_exists()` function that can works in both of the situations covered by `lp_obs()` and `lp_unobs()`. I struggled with this step, mostly due to matching of types and those cascading effects. It sounds from the description like your mu_y1 and mu_y2
are measurements, not parameters.  Or maybe parameters estimated
from measurements?

It'd also make things easier to understand if you named
the variables in your description (C and N) the same thing
as in the model (mu_y1 and mu_y2?).

- Bob

> On Nov 26, 2015, at 10:16 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Thursday, November 26, 2015 at 8:55:31 AM UTC-5, Christoph wrote:
> My (amateurish?) approach was as follows:
>
>   parameters {
>     real mu_y1[Ntotal]; //mean of tech. replicates for first measurement
>     real mu_y2[Ntotal]; //mean of tech. replicates for second measurement
>   }
>
>   transformed parameters {
>     ...
>     real y[Ntotal];
>
>     for(i in 1:Ntotal) {
>       y[i] <- mu_y2[i] - mu_y1[i]; //differences of means
>      }
>     }
>
>   model {
>     mu_y1 ~ normal(...);
>     mu_y2 ~ normal(...);
>
>     for(i in 1:Ntotal) {
>       y[i] ~ ...; // use y in the context of a linear model
>      }
>     }
>
> Of course, the warning message on transformed parameters and Jacobian transforms popped up and created some confusion. As far as I understand the background, this is a linear transform, which makes a correction unnecessary. Am I right in this point?
>
> You are correct that a difference is a linear mapping. If d = a - b, then you have a mapping from (a,b) to (a,d) where d = a - b whose Jacobian matrix is
>
>  1 0
> -1 1
>
> and whose determinant is just 1 * 1 - 0 * (-1) = 1.
>
> However, it does not make sense why you are doing sampling statements for both y[i] and its constituent terms mu_y1[i] and mu_y2[i]. That is not illegal in the Stan language but it is very rarely necessary and yields an incoherent set of posterior beliefs otherwise. I think you can just put priors on mu_y1[i] and mu_y2[i] and use their difference however you want without putting a prior on y[i].
>
> Next, I need to do a very similar analysis on the ratio of the differences in C and N, i.e. I would have a y_C (difference in C measurements) and a y_N (difference in N measurements) and would like to do a linear model on the value of y_C / y_N. Here, my confusion is perfect, as I guess I need a correction here, although a Jacobian matrix in this case would be a 2x1 matrix that does not have a determinant.
>
> It is basically the same as above (and quite possibly unnecessary). You have a mapping from (a,b) to (a,r) where r = a / b whose 2x2 Jacobian matrix is
>
>   1       0
> 1 / b  -a / b^2
>
> whose determinant is 1 * a - 0 / b = a. In that case, you would need to do increment_log_prob(-log(a) - 2 * log(b)).
>
> Ben
>

messages.body_plain:
What's the effective sampling rate and how fast is convergence?
You probably don't need 5000 draws for inference.

It would be a huge speedup if rather than encoding sparse matrices,
you used a long form of the data.  So if you have a sparse matrix x,
the data structure is a table like this:

  x[m, n]  |  m   |  n

where first column is value, and second two columns are indices.  Then
you need the number of entries.  If you can recast the data in this
form, it can be a huge speedup.

The other thing to try other than optimizing the code is to
play with the parameterization.  You can use a non-centered
parameterization where instead of

  alpha ~ normal(mu, sigma);

you use

  alpha_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

  alpha <- sigma * alpha_raw + mu;

and then use alpha as before.  If you have a hierarchical
model with small counts in the groups, this can also have
a very large effect, in some cases leading to models that
will converge where they wouldn't with the centered
parameterization.

You may also find that lowering the initial step size will
help it converge faster during warmup and increasing the target
acceptance rate may help with effective sample size per iteration.
Both cause slower iterations.

- Bob

>
> I think that having 31 year-specific dummy variables in V, and 32 non-hierarchical Omega could be hurting things a bit. But this still seems a lot slower than what I would have hoped for. If it takes 24 hours for this model to run, I guess for 5000 iterations it would take a cool .... 100 days? Ouch.
>
> I should also point out that the last dimension there (the 466) is the number of species. Most of them are observed only a handful of times, so this is quite sparse.
>
> I point out these timings just to emphasize my motivation for speeding the code up. Suggestions are welcome.
>
> Oh, and happy Thanksgiving everyone!
>
> Ryan
>
> On Wednesday, November 25, 2015 at 10:56:04 PM UTC-5, Ryan Batt wrote:

At the end of the code I've included the calculation of metrics that I used to measure speed/ efficiency.
>
> Before I made any changes, the code ran in 33.9 sec. These timings are generally from only 1 trial run. Typically stable within a second or so. Does not include compilation time (see attached code).
>
> Please note: A 1 second savings here could end up saving much more time (hours? days?) when the model is run for more chain iterations (e.g., 5k instead of 50) and for the full data set (but making this extrapolation to full data set is tricky). Currently the array containing species abundance is 3x3x7x15 (for these tests). The full data set is 32x99x13x466 + (that last dimension gets padded with, say, 100+ never-seen species) (and I have similar data sets for 11 regions). So even a little savings in these tests will make a big difference in the end.
>
> Here are the list of changes suggested, in the order that I made the changes, and the associated timings:
> 	• Don't use if() statements to avoid going into a loop when K=0; `for (k in 1:0) {` will skip the loop anyway.
> 		• 34.4 sec
> 		• (I hadn't started doing seconds/ effective sample size yet)
> 	• Move `1 ~ Bernoulli(Omega[t])` out a few levels of for() loops, using `increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(1, Omega[t]) * N * sum(nK[t]))` instead
> 		• 33.4 sec
> 		• (didn't calculate efficiency)
> 	• vectorize `alpha[u,s] ~ normal(` and similar for beta; Thought this would require transpose, but it didn't
> 		• 31.6 sec
> 		• 0.89 sec per sample (denominator is average nEff across all parameters; see attached)

> 		• 32.8 sec
> 		• 0.87 sec per sample
> 	• Make Psi and Theta local variables that are no longer tracked or reported in end (I can recalculate on my own if needed)
> 		• 31.6 sec
> 		• 0.52 sec per sample
> 	• Use matrix algebra for calculating each Psi and Theta (no transpose needed). Used `block()` to adapt the size of covariate matrix (U or V) to the number of K in that site-year, so not wasting computations for when `Kmax` is much larger than most `nK[,]` (in some cases there are ~100 K, but only for 1 site-year, e.g.). Avoids many empty elements of Psi and Theta, too.
> 		• 29.0 sec
> 		• 0.48 sec per sample
> 	• Try vectorizing the calculation of log probabilities. To do this, I decided to aggregate my process covariates (U) over the sample (K) dimension. Then I tried creating vectorized form of the `lp_obs()` function (`lp_obs2()`), and created a new `lp_exists()` function that can works in both of the situations covered by `lp_obs()` and `lp_unobs()`. I struggled with this step, mostly due to matching of types and those cascading effects. I had made some intermediate changes when working towards this that I didn't save, but were a fair bit faster, but didn't include my attempt to vectorize the `lp_obs()` functions. But I forget exactly what I'd had.
> 		• 22.9 sec
> 		• 0.72 sec per sample
> 	• I have not implemented this yet: Make Omega hierarchical, and/or put it on logit scale (see Bob comments)
> As you can see, things have improved. I struggled a lot with #7, and as a result I am hesitant to attempt a similar vectorization for the never-seen species.
>

Along those lines, many of the container formats I chose were the result of iterative trial and error; it was hard to get everything to match up correctly for the functions, but I'm learning.
>
> I would greatly appreciate any further comments, but I understand that I may be asking a lot, and I'm very happy with the feedback I've gotten thus far. Thank you all.
>
> -Ryan

> On Nov 26, 2015, at 4:45 AM, David Mawdsley <dm1...@bristol.ac.uk> wrote:
>
>
>
> On Friday, 20 November 2015 19:53:30 UTC, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> We do not recommend uniform(0, 10) priors, but if you insist
> on using them, you have to make the constraints match, as in:
>
>   real<lower=0, upper=10> sigma;
>
> At which point, you don't need the uniform(0, 10) thing as
> the default is uniform on values satisfying constraints.
>
>
> Thanks.. noted. I've also tried half normal(0,10) and half cauchy(0,5) and exponential(0.1) distributions on the parameter.
>
> The problem with values getting close to 0 is that they're
> log transformed, so they can underflow pretty easily if that's
> where there's support in the model.
>
>
> Is there a way of handling this in Stan?  Running the model in WinBUGs confirms there is support for sigma_delta to be (very close to) 0.

Are you getting different posterior estimates for quantiles
in WinBUGS and Stan?

Are the divergent iterations during warmup or later?

One way to mitigate the problem is smaller stepsize initially
and higher target acceptance rate.  In RStan, I think it's

  control = list(stepsize=0.01, adapt_delta=0.95)

or something like that.  Or even 0.001 and 0.99 if you still
have problems.  That lowers step size and makes the first-order
approximation to the posterior through the gradient more accurate.

There are boundary-avoiding priors that will keep estimates
away from 0, even in maximum likelihood settings.  In realistic
settings, we try to use prior knowledge about the parameter.

- Bob

On Thursday, November 26, 2015 at 11:57:46 AM UTC-5, Wilmar Igl wrote:
> I am using a somewhat different parametrization of a Bayesian hierarchical model for the schools data (compared to the Rstan tutorial) and get exceptions and warnings about divergent transitions, even after adjusting adapt_delta to 0.99 (see Model, Command, Output below). How should I interpret this and deal with it?

I would interpret this as saying the parameterization you are using is less amenable to HMC as the one in the RStan tutorial. The parameterization of the 8 schools model is not best for all hierarchical models, but it often is. You could increase adapt_delta more, but not all problems with divergent transitions can be overcome with a higher target acceptance probability. You need to look at the pairs() plot like the warning suggests to see where the numerical problems are occurring. Divergent transitions near the mode (particularly that have a high probability of being accepted and plotted in the upper triangle) can usually be squashed with a sufficiently high adapt_delta, while divergent transitions in the tail (particularly that have a low probability of being accepted and plotted in the lower triangle) often mean that you should try to reparameterize the model, which is likely in your case.

Ben

P.S. You should also update your version of rstan.

messages.body_plain:
Since you said you had *sparse* data (I take "sparse" to mean
a matrix with lots of zeroes that then get multiplying by other
things to produce more zeros), it led me to *guess*
that you could do it more efficiently than coding it up as
matrices.  The problem with sparse matrix operations using
dense matrices is all the multiply-by-zero and add-zero operations.
Each of these adds to the expression graph, which then takes
time during automatic differentiation to compute gradients.

We're getting far too much mail now for me to have time to
go through everyone's code closely.  Sorry about that.

The difference in chain speeds is almost always due to failures
to find the typical set (volume of high posterior mass) efficiently
during warmup.  The chain will wander off into an area
of high curvature and have to take the step size down to a very
small value to move, which then requires lots of steps elsewhere.
The real problem is that in some cases, Stan can't find its
way back to the typical set (volume of high posterior mass).
You can usually see this in the marginal trace plots of the parameters.

- Bob

Including the 0's definitely means that the object itself will take up much more memory, as it will repeat the information  contained in the array's dimension names. On the other hand, I'm less certain about what to do with a database representation that doesn't have all of the year-site-sample-species combinations encoded in the identifying columns. My lack of understanding is probably because I don't have a clear vision of the desired implementation. Sorry for my slowness here.

> parameterization.
>
> You may also find that lowering the initial step size will
> help it converge faster during warmup and increasing the target

On Thursday, November 26, 2015 at 10:00:41 AM UTC-5, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Thursday, November 26, 2015 at 8:42:27 AM UTC-5, Craig Wang wrote:
> > My question is: I'm going to call the same *.stan file 1,000 times for different simulated data, is there a way to only call the C++ translation once to save time?
>
> Yes, in RStan and PyStan. In RStan, it should not compile the same model repeatedly within the same R session, but you can have it not compile repeatedly across R sessions by first calling

Just to be picky and because I love CmdStan, this is trivial from the terminal using CmdStan as well! Krzysztof

>
> rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
>
> In both RStan and PyStan, you can pass an existing object produced by stan() to the fit argument of stan() to use the same model with different data.
>
> > sample code:
> >
> > for (i in 1:1000){
> >   dat <- data[[i]]
> >   m2 <- stan(file="model.stan", data=dat,iter=100000, chains=1,thin=10)
> >   var[i]<-1-mean(m2@sim$samples[[1]]$var)
> >   }
>
> With Stan, we do not recommend doing 100000 iterations, one chain, or thinning like you might do with a Gibbs sampler or Metropolis-Hastings. The default arguments are more than fine the vast majority of the time. You should read about the differences between how Stan does MCMC relative to a Gibbs sampler or Metropolis-Hastings before doing a bunch of simulations. Also, we do not recommend using syntax like @sim$samples[[1]]$. Use mean(extract(m2, pars = "var", permuted = FALSE)) or something.
>
> Ben
>

> small value to move, which then requires lots of steps elsewhere.

> way back to the typical set (volume of high posterior mass).

messages.body_plain:
I didn't understand the X axis in that plot --- it's labeled
"chain".

What you want to look at is the curvature (or at least
the derivative).  Stan follows the gradient and adapts a step
size to let it move.  Often this is problematic when the
curvature varies a lot over the posterior.  When you get near
a constraint boundary, the transform can be problematic (for
instance, log(epsilon) as epsilon -> 0).

You said you were keeping the upper-bound constraint on g_3,
but I don't see it --- you just have lower=0.  Was that intentional?

- Bob

> On Nov 25, 2015, at 5:01 PM, Michael Thomson <michaelj...@btinternet.com> wrote:
>
>  I think perhaps it would be best if I describe a 1-parameter model with the parameter which I would like to constrain and the results I've gotten attempting to fit this.
>
> So this 1d model has mean (in R)
>
> g_only_model<-function(V,g){
>   P<-1+1/((10V-g)^6)
>   return(P)
> }
>
> with additive Gaussian distributed noise with mean zero and standard deviation sigma.
>
> Using these true values for g and sigma,
>
> g_true=0.5
> sigma_true=0.0001
>
> I've produced synthetic data from this model in R as follows
>
> V<-seq(0.105,2.24,length.out=100)
> P<-simple_eos(V,g.true)+rnorm(length(V),0,sigma.true)
>

> Now previously when fitting this parameter I had used a uniform(0,1) prior, but I know from our previous correspondence that it is best to avoid hard constraints where possible. Now dropping the constraint at 0 is no issue, but the upper bound, at 1, stops singularities appearing in the model and so we wish to keep it. I've done the reparameterisation , g_2=1-g, so that the constraint is g_new>0. Then I understand that the transformation stan applies the log transform to a parameter constrained to be positive. From Bob's previous post in this topic I know that we want parameters to be roughly unit scale in the unconstrained space so I make the further transformation g_3=(exp(1)/0.5)*g_2. Then g_3_true=exp(1) and log(g_3_true)=1, and so g_3 is unit scale in the unconstrained space.

>
> I code my model in terms of g_3 in stan as follows (using an exponential(0.5) prior on g_3),
>
>   data {
>     int<lower=0> N;
>     vector[N] V;
>     vector[N] P;
>     real<lower=0> sigma;
>   }
>   parameters {
>     real<lower=0> g_3;
>   }
>   model{
>     vector[N] mu;
>     g ~ exponential(0.5);
>     for (n in 1:N) mu[n] <- 1 + 1/((10*V[n]-1+(0.5/e())*g_3)^6);
>     P ~ normal(mu, sigma);
>   }
>
> Now fitting this model in stan and increasing adapt_delta and max_treedepth as prompted I get the traceplot shown in the attached file g_only_model_pt5.png. You'll note that a significant number of the chains drift towards the true value but do not converge.
>
> Now if I produce synthetic data with a smaller true value of g, say 0.2, and fit the same model, the results are much better every chain converges as shown by g_only_model_pt2.png. Smaller values of g are farther away from the constraint on g_3, so is this an issue with having a true value for the parameter which is nearer the constraint?
>
> Any feedback anyone could offer would be much appreciated.
> Thanks,
> Michael

> > > It would be a huge speedup if rather than encoding sparse matrices,
> > > you used a long form of the data.  So if you have a sparse matrix x,
> > > the data structure is a table like this:
> > >
> > >   x[m, n]  |  m   |  n
> > >
> > > where first column is value, and second two columns are indices.  Then
> > > you need the number of entries.  If you can recast the data in this
> > > form, it can be a huge speedup.
> > >
> > > The other thing to try other than optimizing the code is to
> > > play with the parameterization.  You can use a non-centered
> > > parameterization where instead of
> > >
> > >   alpha ~ normal(mu, sigma);
> > >
> > > you use
> > >
> > >   alpha_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
> > >
> > >   alpha <- sigma * alpha_raw + mu;
> > >
> > > and then use alpha as before.  If you have a hierarchical
> > > model with small counts in the groups, this can also have
> > > a very large effect, in some cases leading to models that
> > > will converge where they wouldn't with the centered
> > > parameterization.
> > >
> > > You may also find that lowering the initial step size will
> > > help it converge faster during warmup and increasing the target
> > > acceptance rate may help with effective sample size per iteration.

>
> Are you getting different posterior estimates for quantiles
> in WinBUGS and Stan?
>

Slightly; running the model with a half normal prior on delta, mean 0, standard deviation 10, I get 2.5%, 50%, 97.5% estimates from Stan of:
0.031 0.139 0.320
In WinBUGS with the same prior I get:
0.008 0.125 0.313

> Are the divergent iterations during warmup or later?
>

These are all post warmup (I don't think rstan reports warmup ones).

> One way to mitigate the problem is smaller stepsize initially
> and higher target acceptance rate.  In RStan, I think it's
>
>   control = list(stepsize=0.01, adapt_delta=0.95)
>
> or something like that.  Or even 0.001 and 0.99 if you still
> have problems.  That lowers step size and makes the first-order
> approximation to the posterior through the gradient more accurate.
>

This does help a bit; with stepsize=0.001, adapt_delta=0.99 I get fewer divergent transitions (25 vs 107), and get results closer to WinBUGS's:

0.017 0.131 0.314

> There are boundary-avoiding priors that will keep estimates
> away from 0, even in maximum likelihood settings.  In realistic
> settings, we try to use prior knowledge about the parameter.
>

Based on prior knowledge it's quite likely its value is 0*, in which case we'd do a fixed-effect meta-analysis, and avoid the issue.  But it also looks like there's quite a lot of support for it being >0. So I'm not sure what the right thing to do would be, given Stan is going to struggle unless we pull it away from 0 via the prior. Using WinBUGS or JAGS seems a bit of a cop-out, but I think it's the route I'll have to go down for now.

Thanks again for your help with this. It's been really useful in working out what's going on.

David

* Turner et al. (2012) <http://ije.oxfordjournals.org/content/41/3/818>  reported 57% of a large sample of meta-analyses had a between study variance of 0 using the method of moments to estimate it.

On Friday, November 27, 2015 at 11:34:13 AM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:

> The non-centered parameterization is likely going to be a huge
> effect on performance so I’d focus on that first.  And remember
> that the ultimate measure of performance is ESS / time.
>
> On Nov 27, 2015, at 4:17 PM, Ryan Batt <bat...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > No worries at all, Bob. You've been quite gracious with your time and advice! I am very appreciative.
> >
> > Your explanations have given me some insight. I'll a couple other strategies for optimizing/ reformulating the code.
> >
> > For the (potential) benefit of others who may stumble upon this post, I'll be sure to update my code/ strategies. Eventually when this analysis is ready for publication, I'll share more content as well.
> >
> > Thanks again.
> >
> > -Ryan
> >
> > On Thursday, November 26, 2015 at 4:20:31 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > Since you said you had *sparse* data (I take "sparse" to mean
> > > a matrix with lots of zeroes that then get multiplying by other
> > > things to produce more zeros), it led me to *guess*
> > > that you could do it more efficiently than coding it up as
> > > matrices.  The problem with sparse matrix operations using
> > > dense matrices is all the multiply-by-zero and add-zero operations.
> > > Each of these adds to the expression graph, which then takes
> > > time during automatic differentiation to compute gradients.
> > >
> > > We're getting far too much mail now for me to have time to
> > > go through everyone's code closely.  Sorry about that.
> > >
> > > The difference in chain speeds is almost always due to failures
> > > to find the typical set (volume of high posterior mass) efficiently
> > > during warmup.  The chain will wander off into an area
> > > of high curvature and have to take the step size down to a very
> > > small value to move, which then requires lots of steps elsewhere.
> > > The real problem is that in some cases, Stan can't find its
> > > way back to the typical set (volume of high posterior mass).
> > > You can usually see this in the marginal trace plots of the parameters.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > > > On Nov 26, 2015, at 4:05 PM, Ryan Batt <bat...@gmail.com <http://gmail.com/>> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > The effective sample size varies a lot among parameters. With the 50 iterations, some parameters have hundreds, while others are in the single digits. I could provide a more detailed summary of results, though.
> > > >
> > > > From my initial tests, some parameters seemed to converge rather quickly. But I didn't look at all of them, just a smattering.
> > > >
> > > > I'm honestly pretty confused by how to take advantage of the database representation that you suggest. Am I supposed to drop the 0's from that representation? Including the 0's definitely means that the object itself will take up much more memory, as it will repeat the information  contained in the array's dimension names. On the other hand, I'm less certain about what to do with a database representation that doesn't have all of the year-site-sample-species combinations encoded in the identifying columns. I remember the section in the manual. I remember thinking it would be challenging to code up correctly, but do-able. I would appreciate some elaboration on the topic, if you don't mind. Particularly, you seem very confident in the speed increase, but I don't understand why this would happen. My lack of understanding is probably because I don't have a clear vision of the desired implementation. Sorry for my slowness here.
> > >
> > > > I'll try the other suggestions about non-centered distributions and tweaking function arguments. Thank you again, very much.
> > > >
> > > > I'll post the results from the full data set run when it's finished. Just in terms of convergence, etc. Right now the chains are between 40% and 90% complete. That's another question: why are the chains showing such different run times? This question clearly illustrates my lack of understanding of what's going on under the hood. I'd enjoy reading more about what leads to the chains sampling at such different rates.
> > > >
> > > > Thanks!!
> > > >
> > > > -Ryan
> > > >
> > > > On Thursday, November 26, 2015 at 10:50:31 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > What's the effective sampling rate and how fast is convergence?
> > > > You probably don't need 5000 draws for inference.
> > > >
> > > > It would be a huge speedup if rather than encoding sparse matrices,
> > > > you used a long form of the data.  So if you have a sparse matrix x,
> > > > the data structure is a table like this:
> > > >
> > > >   x[m, n]  |  m   |  n
> > > >
> > > > where first column is value, and second two columns are indices.  Then
> > > > you need the number of entries.  If you can recast the data in this
> > > > form, it can be a huge speedup.
> > > >
> > > > The other thing to try other than optimizing the code is to
> > > > play with the parameterization.  You can use a non-centered
> > > > parameterization where instead of
> > > >
> > > >   alpha ~ normal(mu, sigma);
> > > >
> > > > you use
> > > >
> > > >   alpha_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
> > > >
> > > >   alpha <- sigma * alpha_raw + mu;
> > > >
> > > > and then use alpha as before.  If you have a hierarchical
> > > > model with small counts in the groups, this can also have
> > > > a very large effect, in some cases leading to models that
> > > > will converge where they wouldn't with the centered
> > > > parameterization.
> > > >
> > > > You may also find that lowering the initial step size will
> > > > help it converge faster during warmup and increasing the target
> > > > acceptance rate may help with effective sample size per iteration.
> > > > Both cause slower iterations.
> > > >
> > > > - Bob
> > > >
> > > > > On Nov 26, 2015, at 10:26 AM, Ryan Batt <bat...@gmail.com <http://gmail.com/>> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > Hi all,
> > > > >
> > > > > Small update on timings.
> > > > >
> > > > > I decided to let this model chug on a larger-sized data set (32x99x13x466 + 10 0's , so 476). Same model and stan call as in the previously-attached R script. It's been running for ~12 hours now, and the chains are 44%, 52%, 30%, and 28% done (of only 50 iterations; I'm running this on 4 cores, 1 for each chain).
> > > > >
> > > > > I think that having 31 year-specific dummy variables in V, and 32 non-hierarchical Omega could be hurting things a bit. But this still seems a lot slower than what I would have hoped for. If it takes 24 hours for this model to run, I guess for 5000 iterations it would take a cool .... 100 days? Ouch.
> > > > >
> > > > > I should also point out that the last dimension there (the 466) is the number of species. Most of them are observed only a handful of times, so this is quite sparse.
> > > > >
> > > > > I point out these timings just to emphasize my motivation for speeding the code up. Suggestions are welcome.
> > > > >
> > > > > Oh, and happy Thanksgiving everyone!
> > > > >
> > > > > Ryan
> > > > >
> > > > > On Wednesday, November 25, 2015 at 10:56:04 PM UTC-5, Ryan Batt wrote:
> > > > > Hi all,
> > > > >
> > > > > I've been working to make as many improvements as I could. Thanks to Max and Bob for some insights.
> > > > >
> > > > > I boiled Bob's original suite of comments down to a to-do list of optimizations to try. I re-wrote the call to `stan()` to only do 50 iterations for each chain, so that the code would run quickly for testing. The attached R file includes all changes I've made since the original posting. At the end of the code I've included the calculation of metrics that I used to measure speed/ efficiency.
> > > > >
> > > > > Before I made any changes, the code ran in 33.9 sec. These timings are generally from only 1 trial run. Typically stable within a second or so. Does not include compilation time (see attached code).
> > > > >
> > > > > Please note: A 1 second savings here could end up saving much more time (hours? days?) when the model is run for more chain iterations (e.g., 5k instead of 50) and for the full data set (but making this extrapolation to full data set is tricky). Currently the array containing species abundance is 3x3x7x15 (for these tests). The full data set is 32x99x13x466 + (that last dimension gets padded with, say, 100+ never-seen species) (and I have similar data sets for 11 regions). So even a little savings in these tests will make a big difference in the end.
> > > > >
> > > > > Here are the list of changes suggested, in the order that I made the changes, and the associated timings:
> > > > >         • Don't use if() statements to avoid going into a loop when K=0; `for (k in 1:0) {` will skip the loop anyway.
> > > > >                 • 34.4 sec
> > > > >                 • (I hadn't started doing seconds/ effective sample size yet)
> > > > >         • Move `1 ~ Bernoulli(Omega[t])` out a few levels of for() loops, using `increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(1, Omega[t]) * N * sum(nK[t]))` instead
> > > > >                 • 33.4 sec
> > > > >                 • (didn't calculate efficiency)
> > > > >         • vectorize `alpha[u,s] ~ normal(` and similar for beta; Thought this would require transpose, but it didn't
> > > > >                 • 31.6 sec
> > > > >                 • 0.89 sec per sample (denominator is average nEff across all parameters; see attached)
> > > > >         • use tighter priors than cauchy(0, 2.5); I did cauchy(0,2) on the sd, and cauchy(0,1) on the mu; originally tried cauchy(0,1) for both, but that was slower/ less efficient than current
> > > > >                 • 32.8 sec
> > > > >                 • 0.87 sec per sample
> > > > >         • Make Psi and Theta local variables that are no longer tracked or reported in end (I can recalculate on my own if needed)
> > > > >                 • 31.6 sec
> > > > >                 • 0.52 sec per sample
> > > > >         • Use matrix algebra for calculating each Psi and Theta (no transpose needed). Used `block()` to adapt the size of covariate matrix (U or V) to the number of K in that site-year, so not wasting computations for when `Kmax` is much larger than most `nK[,]` (in some cases there are ~100 K, but only for 1 site-year, e.g.). Avoids many empty elements of Psi and Theta, too.
> > > > >                 • 29.0 sec
> > > > >                 • 0.48 sec per sample
> > > > >         • Try vectorizing the calculation of log probabilities. To do this, I decided to aggregate my process covariates (U) over the sample (K) dimension. Then I tried creating vectorized form of the `lp_obs()` function (`lp_obs2()`), and created a new `lp_exists()` function that can works in both of the situations covered by `lp_obs()` and `lp_unobs()`. I struggled with this step, mostly due to matching of types and those cascading effects. I had made some intermediate changes when working towards this that I didn't save, but were a fair bit faster, but didn't include my attempt to vectorize the `lp_obs()` functions. messages.body_plain:
Update:

Doing the non-centered parameterization was a massive speed-up (~20-30 fold).
I noticed that I made an error in my most recent version of the model, after aggregating the presence process to the site level (still incrementing log_inv_logit(logit_psi) for each sample, instead of just 1 time per site).

For a similar reason, I think I also needed to change increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(1, Omega[t]) * N * sum(nK[t])); to increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(1, Omega[t]) * N * sum(nKJt]));; i.e., do 1~Omega[t] J*T times, not also incrementing for each sample K in each site J.

I’m currently working on correcting the above mistakes. I’m also going to aggregate the presence covariates, but then model them as ~normal(mean(covariate), sd(covariate)) so that I don’t lose all of the variability when I aggregate.
​

messages.subject: Trouble with multivariate probit
messages.subject_clean: Trouble with multivariate probit
messages.body_plain:
I am having trouble getting running a very simple multivariate probit model in Stan. It has no predictors, just the intercept. Essentially, you have

    for (i in 1:N)
        y[i] ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);

with the observed data z[i] being a vector of 0's and 1's, with z[i,k] = 1 if y[i,k] > 0 and z[i,k] = 0 if y[i,k] < 0. I have attached two different implementations I have tried: mvprobit1.stan is the most straightforward, and mvprobit.stan is an attempted optimization of the model.

I have tested both implementations using chains = 4, iter = 4000, with synthetic data generated as follows:

    K <- 5
    N <- 10000
    mu <- c(-0.3, +0.6, -1.5, +1.7, 0.0)
    rho <- 0.4
    Sigma <- (1 - rho) * diag(K) + matrix(rho, nrow = K, ncol = K)  # unit variances, correlations of 0.4
    Z <- t(MASS::mvrnorm(N, mu, Sigma) > 0) + 0
    data <- list(
      K = K,
      N = N,
      z = Z,
      eta = 1,
      sigma_mu = 5
    )

The straightforward implementation (mvprobit1.stan) performs miserably: lp__ has an Rhat of 2.11 and n_eff of 3. The optimized implementation performs somewhat better, but still very badly -- if I remember correctly, Rhat is 1.4 or thereabouts, and n_eff is around 17 for lp__.

Any thoughts on why this model is so troublesome for Stan, and what I can do to make it run better?

On Saturday, November 28, 2015 at 8:48:15 PM UTC-5, Kevin Van Horn wrote:
> I remain puzzled as to why multivariate probit appears to be so difficult for Stan, and what, if anything, I can do to get better performance.

The dependence between the latent variables and the common parameters. I wouldn't focus too much on lp__ because its tails are very heavy in this case, but the overall performance is poor by Stan standards, even though the divergent transitions can be eliminated with a sufficiently high adapt_delta. Take a look at

pairs(stanfit, pars = c("L", "lp__"), las = 1)

for your data and you may see (even after disregarding the fixed margins) some nasty curves. I think you just have to run enough chains / iterations to get a decent n_eff.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] expose_stan_functions / user define function variable scope help
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] expose_stan_functions / user define function variable scope help
messages.body_plain:
Stan uses C/C++/Java-style scoping, so the only variables
in scope in a function body are the function's arguments and
any locals already defined.  It makes functions much more
predictable in terms of their behavior and much easier to
modularize in a standalone way.  If they depended on data,
there'd be no way to call them without a data block and
other variables in scope.

- Bob

messages.subject: How to determine a significant WAIC threshold in a GWAS setting?
messages.subject_clean: How to determine a significant WAIC threshold in a GWAS setting?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan,

I just implemented my model with Stan in a genome-wide association study. It worked great. Detailedly, I have 1 million SNP. I run my model for each of them independently. With that, I computed WAIC to quantify the fitness. Now I have 1 million WAIC quantities. I also have a null model, in which no SNP was included. By subtracting the WAIC quantity of the null model, I have the WAIC differences for each of the SNP, which describes how much the model was improved by including each of the SNP.

How to determine a cutoff for the WAIC differences (or original WAIC) to identify the true association? This is reminiscent of multiple comparison correction of p-value in the frequentist framework.

Can I generate a null distribution of the WAIC by shuffling the genotype of each SNP (permutation), from which to compute a p-value for each of the real WAIC?

Also, given that the full posterior distribution of each SNP's effect size was obtained by sampling, can I simply use the 95% CI and not worry about the multiple comparison issue at all?

Xulong

I haven't found one. I've gone over several papers related to this presentation and done a lot of simulations now to try and sort out the issue. I still get a slight bias in the slope which one would expect when not accounting for measurement error.... but the bias grows when the error on x_obs gets large. I would think that it should be taken care of by the measurement error model!

Here is a simpler version for just a line with some measurement error that I've been playing with:

data{

    int<lower=0> N;           // Number of points

    // Actual data
    vector[N] x_obs;          // x
    vector[N] y_obs;          // y
    real x_sig;          // x error
    real y_sig;          // y error

Hopefully someone knows the answer to what this model should
be doing.  Otherwise, I can run some simulations and try to
track down what's going on if you send us the JAGS model, data
simulator, and your proposed Stan model.

You really want to stay away from those fat gamma priors.
They'll pull your posterior away from where you want it to be.

We also don't recommend hard constraints, like uniform(-5, 5),
but if you insist on using them, you need to make sure the parameters
are declared with <lower=-5, upper=5> so that every value satisfying
the constraints has support (density > 0) in the model.

Also, you have to be careful with the notion of "bias" in a Bayesian
setting.  For example, adding a prior to a parameter trades variance
for some bias in finite samples.  Same thing happens with
regularization in a penalized MLE setting.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Bias compared to what?  There’s no guarantee that any posterior summary (mean, median, etc)
will yield an unbiased estimator with respect to the true data generating process, nor does Bayes
claim on to exist.

When the measurement error grows then the covariates get washed out, and for all intents and
purposes you’re fitting a constant, which will pull the slope towards zero.  Is that the bias you’re
seeing?  The beta being too small?  Again that is entirely expected when you have measurement
errors that large.

messages.body_snippet:
Bias compared to what?  There’s no guarantee that any posterior summary (mean, median, etc)
will yield an unbiased estimator with respect to the true data generating process, nor does Bayes
claim on t

> You really want to stay away from those fat gamma priors.
> They'll pull your posterior away from where you want it to be.

> but if you insist on using them, you need to make sure the parameters
> are declared with <lower=-5, upper=5> so that every value satisfying

> setting.  For example, adding a prior to a parameter trades variance
> for some bias in finite samples.  Same thing happens with

messages.body_plain:
Those gamma priors have most of their mass outside the
area where you expect the parameters to be.  See our manual
for basic recommendations, or Gelman et al.'s Bayesian Data Analysis
book, or Andrew's paper:

  Gelman, A. (2006). Prior distributions for variance parameters in hierarchical models.
  Bayesian Analysis, 1(3):515–534

for more analysis.

- Bob

The beta is too small. So it is being pulled toward zero. I've seen more advanced approaches to this (Kelly (2007) if you are familiar) that nail beta well with the same data.... but there is a growing bias in beta towards zero. Just smaller than my approach here. But maybe the answer is just that, with growing error in x_obs, you can't get away from being pulled towards zero... depressing, but honest. I'll keep playing and post the papers in a few moments.

messages.body_plain:
> The beta is too small. So it is being pulled toward zero. I've seen more advanced approaches to this (Kelly (2007) if you are familiar) that nail beta well with the same data.... but there is a growing bias in beta towards zero. Just smaller than my approach here. But maybe the answer is just that, with growing error in x_obs, you can't get away from being pulled towards zero... depressing, but honest. I'll keep playing and post the papers in a few moments.

I wouldn’t say it’s depressing — it’s a proper quantification of uncertainty which should
be exciting!  Ultimately you don’t want to compare any posterior-derived point estimate
of beta to the truth but rather the entire posterior distribution.  For example, it’s a much
fairer comparison to see if a 90% credible interval (between the 5% and 95% quantiles)
captures the true value of beta most of the time.  In the large measurement error case
the posterior mean of beta might be drawn to zero but the posterior itself will widen to
reflect the growing uncertainty, which is exactly what we want!  The only way to get
better inferences is to introduce more information, and if that data can’t be measured
any better than that would have to mean a different likelihood or priors.

Kelly (2007) is an entirely different beast which uses a mixture of Gaussian amongst
other bells and whistles, so it’s really a proper comparison.  You can build this model
in Stan no problem and then you should at least get consistent results (although you
might not — HMC tends to identify bad fits much better than Random Walk Metropolis
and Gibbs).

messages.body_plain:
Ok, so after reading the recommended articles and trusting your advice on what I should expect (paying attention to HDIs instead of nailing point estimates) I think this issue is solved. The astrophysical literature based off papers related to the the comic sans presentation posted earlier endorsed this Inv. Gamma prior a lot but the arguments in Gellman make more sense. Thanks all for your help and I will be sure to give some credit in the acknowledgements in the publication I'm working on.

Cheers!

On Monday, November 30, 2015 at 10:10:26 PM UTC+1, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>
> > The beta is too small. So it is being pulled toward zero. I've seen more advanced approaches to this (Kelly (2007) if you are familiar) that nail beta well with the same data.... but there is a growing bias in beta towards zero. Just smaller than my approach here. But maybe the answer is just that, with growing error in x_obs, you can't get away from being pulled towards zero... depressing, but honest. I'll keep playing and post the papers in a few moments.
>
> I wouldn’t say it’s depressing — it’s a proper quantification of uncertainty which should
> be exciting!  Ultimately you don’t want to compare any posterior-derived point estimate
> of beta to the truth but rather the entire posterior distribution.  For example, it’s a much
> fairer comparison to see if a 90% credible interval (between the 5% and 95% quantiles)
> captures the true value of beta most of the time.  In the large measurement error case
> the posterior mean of beta might be drawn to zero but the posterior itself will widen to
> reflect the growing uncertainty, which is exactly what we want!  The only way to get
> better inferences is to introduce more information, and if that data can’t be measured
> any better than that would have to mean a different likelihood or priors.
>
> Kelly (2007) is an entirely different beast which uses a mixture of Gaussian amongst
> other bells and whistles, so it’s really a proper comparison.  You can build this model
> in Stan no problem and then you should at least get consistent results (although you
> might not — HMC tends to identify bad fits much better than Random Walk Metropolis
> and Gibbs).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Matching the results of a STAN ODE model with a different ODE solver?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Matching the results of a STAN ODE model with a different ODE solver?
messages.body_plain:
I don't think there's anything at all tricky about it.  You
just need to write the diff eqs as a Stan function and provide
the data and parameters as data.  Then you'll get the same answers
to within tolerance as any other working ODE solver (at least for
non-stiff cases Stan can solve).

- Bob

P.S.  It's "Stan", not "STAN", unless you're shouting.

Since I'm more comfortable with the (simpler) DeSolve setup, I'm guessing it's the STAN model that I'm mis-understanding, and therefore mis-specifying. I'd like to be able to match the results.

(Silly simple example: If I have three quantities that are multiplied to generate the data, I should be able to .estimate their product, even if I can't estimate the individual values.
>

>
> You sent us a Stan model that involves an ODE, whereas deSolve is
